pitfalls: Giving antihistamine or steroid first and delaying adrenaline.
IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest.
Missing anaphylaxis without a rash (absent in up to 20%).
Sitting the patient up.
Discharging early without a risk-based observation period or auto-injector.
keyPoints: If in doubt, give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the thigh.
Repeat after 5 minutes if not better; after two doses, start an IV adrenaline infusion.
Lie the patient flat; never stand a hypotensive patient up.
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
Tryptase at 1–2 h, refer to allergy, auto-injector on discharge.

content.specialty: Emergency Medicine and Allergy and Immunology

redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness or tongue swelling: impending airway obstruction; most experienced person to intubate early
No improvement after two doses of IM adrenaline: refractory anaphylaxis; call critical care and start an IV adrenaline infusion
Patient on a beta-blocker with poor response: give glucagon
Never sit or stand a hypotensive patient up
symptoms: Sudden onset over minutes after a trigger (drug, food, insect sting, contrast, vaccine). Parenteral triggers act fastest.
Breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hoarseness; dizziness or collapse.
Abdominal cramps, vomiting, incontinence; anxiety or 'sense of impending doom'.
Skin and mucosal changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema) in over 80%, but absent in up to 20%.
precipitants: Drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast, anaesthetic agents), blood products, vaccines.
physicalSigns: Airway: lip, tongue or throat swelling, hoarseness, stridor.
Breathing: tachypnoea, wheeze, fatigue, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92%, confusion.
Circulation: pale, clammy, hypotension, tachycardia (bradycardia is a late, pre-arrest sign), drowsiness or coma.
Skin: urticaria, angioedema, erythema.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Wheeze without skin, circulatory or allergen features; anaphylaxis can look identical (especially in children). If in doubt, give IM adrenaline.
Swelling of lips, tongue or airway without urticaria in a patient on an ACE inhibitor; usually does not respond to adrenaline.
Throat tightness and stridor without objective allergic features; does not respond to adrenaline.
Bradycardia, pallor, quick recovery when lying flat; no urticaria, wheeze or angioedema.
Hyperventilation, tingling; no hypotension, hypoxia, wheeze or rash. Can be hard to separate in people with previous anaphylaxis.
Skin or mucosal changes only, without airway, breathing or circulation problems: not anaphylaxis.

pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a serious, rapid-onset systemic hypersensitivity reaction that compromises the airway, breathing and/or circulation. Mast cell and basophil mediators cause airway oedema, bronchospasm, vasodilation, capillary leak and sometimes myocardial depression.
keyMechanisms: Airway and breathing: tissue oedema and smooth-muscle contraction cause laryngeal swelling, bronchospasm and wheeze (commonest in food-induced anaphylaxis).

Circulation: vasodilation plus capillary leak causes distributive and hypovolaemic shock; up to 35% of blood volume can leak out within 10 minutes. Myocardial depression and ischaemic ECG changes can occur even with normal coronaries.
Posture: sitting or standing a hypotensive patient reduces venous return and has caused cardiovascular collapse and death; keep them supine (or semi-recumbent if breathless).

Why adrenaline works: alpha effects reverse vasodilation and oedema; beta effects open the airways, increase myocardial contraction and suppress mast-cell mediator release. Delay is linked to protracted and fatal reactions.
Biphasic reactions (about 5%): symptoms recur hours later without re-exposure; median time about 12 h.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise, call for help, remove the trigger
actions: ABCDE approach; call for help (resuscitation team).
Stop the suspected drug, infusion or colloid; remove the trigger if possible.
Lie the patient flat with legs raised (semi-recumbent if breathing is difficult). Do not sit or stand them up.

clinicalManagement.title: IM adrenaline first
actions: Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM into the anterolateral mid-thigh: RCUK 0.5 mg (0.5 mL) for adults and children over 12; MOH 0.3–0.5 mg.
Repeat after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist (MOH: every 5–15 min as needed).
Do not give IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest or specialist hands.
Immediate intubation by the most experienced available operator.
branches.condition: Impending airway obstruction (angioedema, stridor)

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen and fluids
actions: High-flow oxygen (MOH: 8–10 L/min by face mask, up to 100%).
Hypotension or poor response: rapid IV crystalloid bolus 500–1000 mL (RCUK) or 1–2 L 0.9% saline (MOH); repeat as needed. Severe shock may need 3–5 L.
Use IO access if IV access is delayed.

clinicalManagement.title: Persistent bronchospasm
actions: Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulised in 3 mL saline (MOH), or 2–3 puffs MDI; repeat as needed.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory anaphylaxis
actions: Call critical care early; keep giving IM adrenaline every 5 min until the infusion runs.

Start low-dose IV adrenaline infusion: RCUK 1 mg in 100 mL 0.9% NaCl at 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 0.1 microgram/kg/min) via a dedicated line; 1 mL/kg/h if hypotensive or hypoxic. MOH: start at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and titrate.
Continuous ECG, SpO2 and BP at least every 5 min. Titrate to the lowest effective rate.
Wean: halve as symptoms improve; 1 h after full resolution, reduce over 30 min and stop.
If still refractory: noradrenaline (or dopamine per MOH; metaraminol or vasopressin per RCUK) by expert titration.
Glucagon: MOH 1–5 mg IV over 5 min then 5–15 microgram/min infusion (rapid push causes vomiting); RCUK 1 mg IV, repeat or 1–2 mg/h. Hold the beta-blocker.
branches.condition: On a beta-blocker

actions: Atropine 0.5 mg IV, repeat if necessary (RCUK).
branches.condition: Persistent severe bradycardia despite fluids

clinicalManagement.timeframe: No improvement after two IM doses

clinicalManagement.title: Adjuncts after stabilisation (never instead of adrenaline)
actions: Antihistamines are third-line and only for skin symptoms: RCUK prefers a non-sedating oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine). MOH lists cetirizine 10 mg IV or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV, and famotidine 20 mg IV.
Corticosteroids: RCUK does not advise them routinely (consider hydrocortisone 200 mg IV for refractory reactions or coexisting asthma). MOH lists methylprednisolone 125 mg IV.

clinicalManagement.title: Observe and discharge safely
actions: RCUK fast-track discharge after 2 h from resolution only if: good response within 5–10 min to a single dose given within 30 min of onset, complete resolution, already has trained-in-use auto-injectors, and adequate supervision.

At least 6 h after resolution if 2 IM doses were needed or there was a previous biphasic reaction. MOH: observe 6 h if airway compromise, high adrenaline doses, coronary artery disease, asthma, or on beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors.

At least 12 h if more than 2 doses were needed, severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise, possible continuing absorption (e.g. slow-release medicines), late night presentation, or poor access to emergency care.
Before discharge: stand the patient up and check for dizziness; eat something at least 1 h before leaving. If not improving: ICU (MOH).

pathophysiology.summary: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, usually after luminal obstruction (faecolith/appendicolith or lymphoid hyperplasia). Rising pressure causes venous congestion, ischaemia and bacterial invasion of the wall; untreated, it can become gangrenous and perforate, forming a phlegmon, abscess or generalised peritonitis.
keyMechanisms: Visceral (midgut) pain from appendiceal distension is felt periumbilically; when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum the pain localises to the right iliac fossa.
Uncomplicated appendicitis: inflamed without gangrene, perforation or abscess — may resolve with antibiotics (or even spontaneously) in selected patients.
Complicated appendicitis: gangrene, perforation, phlegmon or periappendiceal abscess; an appendicolith predicts failure of non-operative treatment.
Appendiceal neoplasms are found in 3–17% of adults aged 40 or over with complicated appendicitis (WSES).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and risk-stratify
actions: Analgesia (do not withhold for diagnosis); IV fluids if dehydrated; nil by mouth if surgery likely.
Pregnancy test, FBC, CRP, urinalysis.
Calculate AIR or AAS score: low risk — consider discharge with safety-netting; intermediate — observe and image; high risk — surgical review.

clinicalManagement.title: Image when indicated
actions: Ultrasound (POCUS by an experienced operator) first.
Negative or inconclusive ultrasound and still intermediate risk: low-dose contrast CT (adults); MRI in pregnancy.
High risk and under 40: may go straight to diagnostic ± therapeutic laparoscopy.

clinicalManagement.title: Uncomplicated appendicitis
actions: Laparoscopic appendectomy on the next available list, within 24 h (do not delay beyond 24 h).
Single preoperative dose of broad-spectrum antibiotic 0–60 min before incision; NO postoperative antibiotics.
Antibiotic-first (non-operative) option: discuss with selected patients without an appendicolith — recurrence up to 39% at 5 years; start IV then switch to oral. Not advised in pregnancy.

clinicalManagement.title: Complicated appendicitis (gangrene, perforation, peritonitis)
actions: Start antibiotics in the ED after cultures: ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 h + metronidazole 500 mg IV/PO every 8 h (other MOH Table 2 options below).
Severe infection, septic shock, older or immunocompromised: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 h (MOH).
Laparoscopic appendectomy; suction only (no irrigation); no routine drains in adults; routine histopathology.
Postoperative antibiotics: stop after 3–5 days if source control is adequate (WSES); MOH: 24 h if operated within 12–24 h, 4 days with adequate source control. Switch to oral when eating.
Follow the sepsis pathway; antibiotics within the first hour; urgent source control.
branches.condition: Sepsis or septic shock

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Urgently — within 8 h in children (WSES); source control within 24 h (MOH)

clinicalManagement.title: Phlegmon or periappendiceal abscess

Laparoscopic surgery is a safe alternative in experienced hands.
No routine interval appendectomy in under-40s; age 40 or over treated non-operatively: colonoscopy and interval contrast CT (neoplasm risk).

pathophysiology.summary: Bowel obstruction blocks the passage of intestinal contents. Adhesions from previous surgery are the single most common cause of small bowel obstruction; others are incarcerated hernias, tumours, Crohn's disease and volvulus.
keyMechanisms: Proximal to the block, bowel distends with gas and fluid; vomiting and third-space losses cause dehydration, hypokalaemia and acute kidney injury.
Rising intraluminal pressure and twisting (closed loop) compromise venous then arterial flow → strangulation, ischaemia, perforation and peritonitis.
Examination detects strangulation in only about 48% of cases, so imaging and laboratory markers are essential.
Most adhesive obstructions (about 70–90%) settle with non-operative management; recurrence is common.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and assess
actions: IV fluid resuscitation; correct electrolytes (especially potassium); monitor urine output.
Analgesia and antiemetic; nil by mouth.
Nasogastric tube decompression (prevents aspiration).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide: surgery now or non-operative trial

clinicalManagement.title: Non-operative management
actions: Nil by mouth, NG (or long intestinal tube) decompression, fluids, electrolyte correction, nutritional support, aspiration prevention.
Water-soluble contrast with abdominal X-ray at 24 h: contrast in colon = resolving; no contrast = likely failure → surgery.
A 72-h non-operative trial is considered safe; operate if no resolution or any deterioration.

pathophysiology.summary: ACS is myocardial ischaemia from an acute reduction in coronary flow, usually after atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with thrombosis. It includes acute myocardial infarction (troponin rise with ischaemia) and unstable angina. Complete occlusion (STEMI or other 'acute coronary occlusion MI', ACOMI) needs emergency reperfusion.
keyMechanisms: Plaque rupture/erosion exposes thrombogenic material → platelet aggregation and thrombus; partial occlusion gives NSTE-ACS, complete occlusion gives STEMI/ACOMI.
ACOMI includes ECG patterns beyond ST elevation: high lateral, posterior and right ventricular MI, De Winter T waves, and LBBB meeting modified Sgarbossa criteria (Australian 2025).
Myocardial necrosis releases troponin; high-sensitivity assays allow rule-in/rule-out within 1–2 h using assay-specific thresholds and deltas.
Complications: arrhythmia (VF/VT), heart failure, cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications.

clinicalManagement.title: First 10 minutes
actions: ECG within 10 min; continuous monitoring and defibrillator if ongoing symptoms or ischaemic ECG.
Aspirin 300 mg orally (chewed or dissolved) unless contraindicated.
Oxygen only if SpO2 below 90%; keep SpO2 at 96% or lower if oxygen is given.
IV fentanyl or morphine boluses for chest pain if no contraindication.
Exclude aortic dissection when suspected before antithrombotics.

clinicalManagement.title: STEMI / ACOMI — reperfusion
actions: Primary PCI preferred if deliverable within 120 min of first medical contact (NICE: within 120 min of when fibrinolysis could have been given). PCI-capable centre: within 60 min of arrival; transfer: within 90 min of first hospital arrival.
Otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 min of first medical contact, with an antithrombin (UFH or enoxaparin). Age 70 or over: half-dose tenecteplase as part of a pharmaco-invasive strategy.
After fibrinolysis: ECG at 60–90 min — residual ST elevation → immediate angiography (do not repeat lysis); successful lysis → transfer to PCI centre, angiography within 2–24 h.
Primary PCI: DAPT with aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel (clopidogrel if these are contraindicated or on oral anticoagulation); UFH (or bivalirudin). No routine GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor.
Shock within 12 h → angiography ± PCI; no routine IABP or VA-ECMO.

clinicalManagement.title: NSTE-ACS
actions: Anticoagulate: UFH, enoxaparin or fondaparinux (NICE: fondaparinux if no high bleeding risk and not going for immediate angiography; UFH if creatinine above 265 µmol/L).
Very high risk (instability, ongoing pain, shock, heart failure, arrhythmia): immediate invasive strategy within 2 h.
High risk: early invasive within 24 h (Australian); NICE: consider angiography within 72 h if GRACE 6-month mortality above 3.0%.
DAPT: aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel if routine invasive (prasugrel only once anatomy known and PCI intended); selective invasive: ticagrelor or clopidogrel.
Lower risk: ischaemia testing guides need for angiography.

clinicalManagement.title: In-hospital and discharge
actions: DAPT 6–12 months (high ischaemic/low bleeding risk); then long-term P2Y12 inhibitor over aspirin (Australian).
On oral anticoagulation: OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel for 1–4 weeks, then stop aspirin (PPI with triple therapy).
High-intensity lipid lowering: LDL-C below 1.4 mmol/L and at least 50% reduction; beta-blocker if LV impairment; cardiac rehabilitation; vaccinations.

pathophysiology.summary: An exacerbation (ECOPD) is increased dyspnoea and/or cough and sputum worsening over less than 14 days, often with tachypnoea and tachycardia. Airway infection (mostly viral), pollution or other insults increase airway and systemic inflammation, mucus and gas trapping. Dyspnoea is the key symptom.
keyMechanisms: Triggers: respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus) are the main cause; bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis; Pseudomonas in severe or long-standing COPD), fine particulate air pollution and excess heat also trigger events.
Increased airway inflammation and mucus with expiratory flow limitation cause dynamic hyperinflation (gas trapping), increased work of breathing and breathlessness.
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; respiratory muscle fatigue and hypoventilation cause hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis.
High-concentration oxygen and oxygen-driven nebulisers can raise PaCO2 in hypercapnic patients — hence controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92% and air-driven nebulisers.
Sputum or blood eosinophilia marks events that may respond better to systemic steroids.
Recovery takes 7–10 days on average; at 8 weeks up to 20% have not returned to baseline. Frequent exacerbations (2 or more a year) speed lung-function decline.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and setting
actions: Check RR, HR, SpO2, mental status and accessory-muscle use; take ABG with FiO2 recorded.

Treat in hospital if: severe breathlessness, poor or deteriorating condition, cyanosis, worsening oedema, impaired consciousness or confusion, on long-term oxygen, SaO2 below 90%, pH below 7.35, PaO2 below 7 kPa, new X-ray changes, significant comorbidity, rapid onset or not coping at home (NICE Table 7).
Grade hospitalised patients: no respiratory failure; non-life-threatening; or life-threatening respiratory failure (GOLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Controlled oxygen
actions: Venturi mask preferred (more accurate than nasal prongs); titrate to SpO2 88–92%.
Repeat blood gas after starting or changing oxygen to detect rising PaCO2 or falling pH.
High-flow nasal oxygen: ERS advises trialling NIV first in hypercapnic respiratory failure (cited in GOLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Short-acting bronchodilators
actions: Short-acting beta2-agonist (salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergic (ipratropium).
MDI with spacer: 1–2 puffs every hour for 2–3 doses, then every 2–4 h by response (GOLD). Avoid continuous nebulisation.
If nebulised and hypercapnic or acidotic: drive with compressed AIR, give oxygen by nasal cannula at the same time; always prescribe the driving gas (NICE 1.3.11–1.3.12).
Continue or start long-acting bronchodilators as soon as possible before discharge.

clinicalManagement.title: Systemic corticosteroid
actions: Prednisolone 30 mg orally once daily for 5 days (NICE) — GOLD recommends 40 mg prednisone-equivalent for 5 days. Oral is as effective as IV.
Do not exceed 5–7 days (STS: 5–7 days preferred over longer courses).

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics when indicated
actions: Give if all three cardinal symptoms (more dyspnoea, sputum volume and purulence), OR two including purulence, OR needs NIV or invasive ventilation (GOLD).
Empirical choice by local resistance: amoxicillin–clavulanate, macrolide, doxycycline (tetracycline), second-generation cephalosporin, or a respiratory quinolone in selected patients (GOLD, STS).
Duration 5 days (GOLD; STS 5–7 days). Prefer oral when able to swallow.

clinicalManagement.title: Ventilatory support
actions: NIV is first-line for hypercapnic respiratory failure persisting despite optimal medical therapy (NICE 1.3.30; GOLD; STS — ward, HDU or ICU).
Deliver NIV in a dedicated area with trained staff; document a plan for deterioration and the ceiling of treatment before starting.
Stop NIV directly (no weaning needed) once the patient tolerates at least 4 h of unassisted breathing (GOLD).
Invasive ventilation: NIV failure, or contraindication to NIV; decide on functional status, BMI, oxygen need when stable, comorbidities and previous ICU — not age or FEV1 alone (NICE 1.3.34).
Respiratory stimulants (doxapram) only if NIV is unavailable or inappropriate (NICE); GOLD does not recommend them.
Confusion, FiO2 above 40% needed, PaCO2 above 60 mmHg or pH 7.25 or less: senior and ICU review now.

Smoking cessation support.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute heart failure (AHF) is the sudden worsening of heart failure symptoms and signs. Raised left-sided filling pressures push fluid into the lungs (pulmonary oedema); reduced cardiac output causes hypoperfusion. Patients are profiled by congestion (wet/dry) and perfusion (warm/cold).
keyMechanisms: Congestion ('wet'): raised filling pressures → pulmonary congestion, orthopnoea/PND, peripheral oedema, raised JVP, congested liver and gut, ascites.
Hypoperfusion ('cold'): cold sweaty extremities, oliguria, confusion, dizziness, narrow pulse pressure.
'Warm and wet' needs diuresis (± vasodilators); 'cold and wet' needs vasoactive support with diuresis (SHA 2019).
Hypertensive AHF (afterload mismatch) responds to vasodilators; cardiogenic shock needs inotropes/vasopressors and treatment of the cause (e.g. ACS).
Neurohormonal activation (RAAS, sympathetic) drives sodium and water retention; acidosis on blood gas carries a worse prognosis.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and profile
actions: Check airway, breathing (RR, SpO2), BP, perfusion; profile warm/cold and wet/dry.
ECG, chest X-ray, natriuretic peptide, troponin, renal function, electrolytes, FBC, glucose, LFTs, TSH; blood gas if pulmonary oedema, COPD or shock.
Identify triggers: ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, infection, non-adherence, valve disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen and ventilatory support
actions: Oxygen only if SpO2 below 90% or PaO2 below 60 mmHg.

Respiratory distress (RR above 25, SpO2 below 90%): start NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) as soon as possible (SHA); NICE advises NIV for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe dyspnoea and acidaemia, not routinely. Caution — NIV lowers BP.
Intubate if hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis cannot be managed non-invasively, or with exhaustion or reduced consciousness.

clinicalManagement.title: IV loop diuretic
actions: New AHF or not on oral diuretics: furosemide 20–40 mg IV (or equivalent).
On chronic diuretics: initial IV dose at least equivalent to the usual oral dose.
Bolus or infusion; adjust to symptoms, urine output, weight, renal function and electrolytes.
Resistant oedema: add a thiazide-type diuretic or acetazolamide (watch potassium, sodium, BP, renal function).
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 h of first medical contact

clinicalManagement.title: Vasodilators
actions: SHA: IV vasodilators may be considered for symptom relief if SBP above 110 mmHg without symptomatic hypotension; first-line in hypertensive AHF. Monitor BP frequently.

NICE: do not routinely offer nitrates; use in specific circumstances (myocardial ischaemia, severe hypertension, regurgitant aortic/mitral valve disease) with close BP monitoring in level 2 care. Do not use sodium nitroprusside.
Opiates: not routinely (NICE); low-dose only with caution for severe distress (SHA).

clinicalManagement.title: Hypotension and cardiogenic shock
actions: ECG and echocardiography immediately; arterial line; consider transfer to a tertiary centre.
ACS with shock: urgent coronary angiography for revascularisation.
Fluid challenge if no overt overload or volume status uncertain.

Inotrope (dobutamine) for hypoperfusion with SBP 110 mmHg or less not responding to standard treatment; norepinephrine preferred vasopressor if persistent hypoperfusion. Not routinely (mortality concerns).
IABP not routine; short-term mechanical support in refractory shock after heart-team discussion.

pathophysiology.summary: Ischaemic stroke is sudden focal neurological loss from arterial occlusion (thrombosis or embolism). Around the irreversibly infarcted core lies the ischaemic penumbra — tissue that can be saved if blood flow is restored quickly, which is why treatment is time-critical.
keyMechanisms: Causes: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism (atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis), small-vessel (lacunar) disease, arterial dissection and other rarer causes.

Penumbra survival falls with every minute of occlusion; thrombolysis and thrombectomy aim to reperfuse it. Advanced imaging (CT perfusion or MRI) identifies salvageable tissue beyond standard time windows.
Thrombolysis risks symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage — hence strict exclusion of haemorrhage on CT and control of BP to 185/110 mmHg or lower.
Hyperglycaemia, hypoxaemia and fever worsen the injury; aspiration is common with dysphagia.

4.5–9 h (known onset) or wake-up stroke (within 9 h of sleep midpoint): IVT only with CT/MRI core–perfusion mismatch (or DWI-FLAIR mismatch) and when thrombectomy is not planned; plain CT only → no IVT.
No antithrombotics within 24 h after IVT.
Deliver only within an organised stroke service with trained staff and post-thrombolysis protocols.
VKA with unknown INR → no IVT. Dabigatran within 48 h → idarucizumab then IVT may be considered (ESO, 8/9). Factor Xa inhibitors within 48 h → no andexanet-then-IVT.

pathophysiology.summary: AKI is an abrupt fall in kidney function measured by a rise in serum creatinine and/or a fall in urine output. Causes are pre-renal (reduced perfusion), intrinsic renal (tubular, interstitial, glomerular or vascular injury) and post-renal (urinary tract obstruction); several often coexist.
keyMechanisms: Pre-renal: hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure, liver disease and drugs that reduce glomerular perfusion (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, diuretics) lower GFR; prolonged hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic tubular injury.

Intrinsic: acute tubular injury (sepsis, ischaemia, nephrotoxins such as aminoglycosides and iodinated contrast), acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis or vasculitis (haematuria + proteinuria), myeloma.
Post-renal: obstruction (stones, prostate, tumour) raises tubular pressure; bilateral obstruction, obstruction of a solitary kidney or infected obstruction (pyonephrosis) is an emergency.

Consequences: reduced excretion of potassium, acid and water causes hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload and pulmonary oedema; retained uraemic toxins cause pericarditis and encephalopathy.
Creatinine lags behind the fall in GFR, so early AKI may show only oliguria.

clinicalManagement.title: Detect, stage and look for life-threatening complications
actions: Confirm AKI by creatinine rise or oliguria; stage with KDIGO; compare with baseline.
Check potassium, acid–base, fluid status and ECG straight away.
Urine dipstick and record the likely cause in the notes.

clinicalManagement.title: Treat hyperkalaemia (5-step approach)
actions: STEP 1 Protect the heart if ECG changes: 30 mL 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10 min (calcium chloride 10 mL 10% over 5 min in cardiac arrest/peri-arrest). Repeat if ECG changes persist.

STEP 2 Shift K+ into cells: soluble insulin 10 units in 25 g glucose IV (severe; suggested for moderate). If pre-treatment glucose below 7.0 mmol/L, follow with 10% glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h. Add nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg (never alone). No routine IV sodium bicarbonate.
STEP 3 Remove K+: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily for up to 72 h (severe; consider for moderate), or patiromer 8.4 g once daily. Calcium resonium no longer routine.
STEP 4 Monitor: K+ at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h; glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 min after insulin.
STEP 5 Prevent recurrence: stop potassium supplements and drugs that raise potassium; renal or critical care referral if severe or refractory.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately if K+ 6.5 or more or ECG changes

clinicalManagement.title: Restore perfusion
actions: Hypovolaemia: isotonic crystalloid rather than colloid (albumin or starches) (KDIGO 3.1.1).
Shock: vasopressors together with fluids (KDIGO 3.1.2); protocol-based haemodynamic management in septic shock.
Fluid overloaded: no further fluid; loop diuretic only for overload while awaiting RRT or during recovery.

clinicalManagement.title: Stop and adjust drugs
actions: Temporarily stop ACE inhibitors and ARBs (with diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis), NSAIDs, diuretics and other nephrotoxins; avoid aminoglycosides if alternatives exist.
Pharmacist review of all doses for current kidney function.
Do not use loop diuretics to treat AKI itself, or low-dose dopamine (KDIGO 3.4.2, 3.5.1; NICE 1.5.3, 1.5.5).
Do not delay iodinated contrast in an emergency when delay is clinically significant (NICE 1.1.7).

clinicalManagement.title: Find and treat the cause
actions: Obstruction: catheter for bladder outflow; urology referral; nephrostomy or stent within 12 h; immediate referral if pyonephrosis, solitary kidney, bilateral obstruction or complications.
Nephrology within 24 h if: possible vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis or myeloma; no clear cause; poor response; complications; stage 3; transplant; or CKD stage 4–5.

clinicalManagement.title: Renal replacement therapy
actions: Refer immediately when not responding to medical treatment: hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy), fluid overload or pulmonary oedema (NICE 1.5.8).
Decide on the whole clinical picture and trends, not an isolated urea, creatinine or potassium (KDIGO 5.1.2; NICE 1.5.9).
Airway, breathing, circulation or conscious-level problems: critical care team first (UKKA 19.4).

pathophysiology.summary: Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation of the pancreas with acinar cell destruction. Premature activation of digestive enzymes injures the gland and triggers a systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) that can progress to organ failure; severity is defined by organ failure lasting more than 48 h and by local complications such as necrosis.
keyMechanisms: Common causes: gallstones and alcohol; others include hypertriglyceridaemia (above 11.3 mmol/L), hypercalcaemia, drugs, microlithiasis, hereditary and autoimmune pancreatitis, tumours and pancreas divisum (NICE, WSES).
SIRS causes capillary leak and third-space fluid loss → hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration (rising haematocrit), rising urea and AKI; early resuscitation aims to protect pancreatic microcirculation.
Organ failure (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal) persisting more than 48 h defines severe disease; about 1 in 3 such patients die (WSES).
(Peri)pancreatic necrosis develops over days; it is best seen on contrast CT after 72 h. Infection of necrosis peaks in weeks 2–4.
Intra-abdominal hypertension and abdominal compartment syndrome can complicate severe disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and look for the cause
actions: Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase/amylase more than 3× ULN; characteristic imaging.
Ultrasound on admission for gallstones; LFTs; triglycerides and calcium if not biliary or alcohol.
Assess for SIRS and organ failure; calculate BISAP.

clinicalManagement.title: Early goal-directed fluid resuscitation
actions: Start isotonic crystalloids early without waiting for haemodynamic worsening (Ringer's lactate may be preferred; evidence over saline is weak).
Reassess frequently (HR, BP, urine output, haematocrit, urea, creatinine, lactate) — avoid fluid overload.
WSES gives no fixed volume; adjust to age, weight, cardiac and renal function.

clinicalManagement.title: Analgesia
actions: Adequate analgesia for all within 24 h; no evidence for restricting opioids.
Avoid NSAIDs if AKI. Multimodal approach; PCA; epidural in severe cases needing prolonged high-dose opioids.

clinicalManagement.title: Feed early — do not starve
actions: Do not make nil by mouth unless there is a clear reason such as vomiting (NICE).
Moderately severe or severe: enteral nutrition started within 72 h (gastric or jejunal); parenteral only if enteral fails or is contraindicated.

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics only for infection
actions: No prophylactic antibiotics (WSES, NICE, MOH).

Suspected infected necrosis (deterioration, gas in collection, raised procalcitonin): antibiotics that penetrate necrosis covering Gram-negative, Gram-positive and anaerobes — e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h (MOH Table 2 severe regimen); carbapenem only in the very critically ill; quinolones only for beta-lactam allergy.
No routine antifungal prophylaxis.

clinicalManagement.title: Gallstone pancreatitis
actions: Cholangitis → ERCP. CBD obstruction → ERCP. No ERCP for predicted severe biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis or obstruction.
Mild gallstone pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission.

clinicalManagement.title: Organ failure and complications
actions: Organ dysfunction: HDU monitoring; persistent organ failure despite fluids → ICU.
Monitor for intra-abdominal hypertension; limit excess fluids and sedation.

Necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications: seek advice from a specialist pancreatic centre (NICE); endoscopic (or percutaneous) step-up approach for infected necrosis, delaying intervention where possible.
No specific drug therapy beyond organ support and nutrition (WSES).

pathophysiology.summary: Poisoning causes harm through the toxin's specific mechanism (e.g. opioid receptor agonism, GABA potentiation, sympathomimetic excess, hepatotoxic metabolite) plus secondary effects: airway loss and aspiration, hypoventilation, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia or hyperthermia, seizures, arrhythmias and rhabdomyolysis.
keyMechanisms: Opioids: mu-receptor agonism → the overdose triad of pinpoint pupils, unconsciousness and respiratory depression.
Benzodiazepines: GABA-A potentiation → sedation, slurred speech, ataxia; respiratory depression is rare with oral use alone but more likely with IV use or co-ingestion (alcohol, opioids).

Alcohol: CNS depression in proportion to blood level (wide individual variation); hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, aspiration; Wernicke's encephalopathy if glucose is given without thiamine in chronic heavy drinkers.
Psychostimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, Captagon/fenethylline, khat): sympathomimetic excess → agitation, psychosis, hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, ACS, hyperthermia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis.
Paracetamol: excess NAPQI depletes glutathione → centrilobular liver necrosis over 24–72 h; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective when started early.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and assess
actions: Airway, breathing, circulation; protect the airway, intubate and ventilate if needed.
Check glucose, temperature, ECG; hourly GCS; look for a toxidrome.
Get a history of agents, amounts, timing and intent; contact the regional poison control centre.

clinicalManagement.title: Opioid toxicity
actions: Naloxone: start 0.05 mg IV in most patients, increase to 0.4 mg, then 2 mg, then 10 mg as needed (0.4 mg is an appropriate start in non-dependent patients). No response to 10 mg → opioid unlikely.
Goal: reverse respiratory depression without precipitating withdrawal (risk of vomiting and aspiration).
Re-sedation: repeat doses or bolus plus infusion. IM/SC route if no IV (onset delayed 5–15 min after 1 mg).
Discharge only if normal for several hours after naloxone with no other concerns (e.g. suicide risk).

clinicalManagement.title: Benzodiazepine toxicity
actions: Supportive care: oxygen, positioning (not face down), airway protection.
Flumazenil if benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression is suspected; its short half-life requires close observation for several hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Alcohol intoxication
actions: Supportive: airway, glucose and thiamine, treat seizures, gradual rewarming.
Thiamine 100 mg slow IV (over 5 min) or IM before glucose in chronic heavy drinkers; may repeat 50–100 mg every 8 h.
Glucose for coma: 50–100 mL of 50% dextrose (25–50 g) slowly IV. Glucagon is ineffective for alcohol-induced hypoglycaemia.
No activated charcoal for ethanol alone; consider if other toxins ingested. Look for co-ingestants and toxic alcohols.

clinicalManagement.title: Stimulant toxicity (amphetamines, Captagon, cocaine, khat)
actions: Calm environment ('ART': acceptance, reassurance, talk-down); avoid physical restraint if possible.
Benzodiazepines first-line for agitation and cardiovascular/CNS toxicity: diazepam 2–10 mg IV/IM (or 10–30 mg PO) or lorazepam 1–2 mg IV/IM (2–4 mg PO), repeated every 5–10 min until lightly sedated.
Psychosis: haloperidol 5–10 mg PO/IM/IV or risperidone 2–4 mg PO; avoid anticholinergic drugs.

Hypertension/tachycardia not settling with sedation: phentolamine 2–10 mg IV over 10 min; then nitroprusside or nitroglycerin. Avoid beta-blockers and labetalol in stimulant-associated ACS; PCI preferred to lysis.
Temperature above 38.5 °C: active cooling. Seizures: diazepam 5–10 mg or lorazepam 1–2 mg IV over 2 min, repeat as needed; phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg over 20 min.

clinicalManagement.title: Paracetamol overdose
actions: Potentially toxic: 10 g or 200 mg/kg or more (whichever is less) in 24 h; or 12 g / 300 mg/kg over 48 h (repeated supratherapeutic).
Activated charcoal 50 g to a cooperative awake adult within 2 h of a toxic immediate-release ingestion (within 4 h if 30 g or more).
4-h paracetamol level on the nomogram; if the level will not be available until 8 h or later after ingestion, start acetylcysteine while waiting.
Acetylcysteine two-bag regimen: 200 mg/kg (max 22 g) IV over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 11 g) over 16 h. Weight = actual, rounded up to nearest 10 kg, ceiling 110 kg.
Modified-release 10 g/200 mg/kg or more: full acetylcysteine course (nomogram not valid); 30 g/500 mg/kg or more, or level above double the line: increased dose.
Repeat ALT (± paracetamol level) 2 h before the infusion ends; continue if ALT rising or level above 10 mg/L.

pathophysiology.summary: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction. In an attack, smooth-muscle bronchospasm, airway wall oedema and mucus plugging narrow the airways, trap air (dynamic hyperinflation) and cause ventilation–perfusion mismatch.
keyMechanisms: Airway narrowing: smooth-muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and increased mucus secretion; chronic remodelling (smooth-muscle hypertrophy, subepithelial fibrosis) adds fixed narrowing.
Type 2 (eosinophilic) inflammation is the commonest pattern (40–70%): IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IgE and mast-cell mediators; usually steroid-responsive.
Early attack: hyperventilation lowers PaCO2. A normal or rising PaCO2 means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

Death in acute asthma: asphyxia from severe obstruction and mucus plugging, severe auto-PEEP reducing venous return and cardiac output, and arrhythmia (risk raised by hypokalaemia and QT prolongation from high-dose beta-agonists).
Most deaths occur in chronically uncontrolled asthma with under-use of inhaled steroids and deterioration over days.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and start treatment at once
actions: Assess dyspnoea, RR, HR, SpO2 and PEF; classify as moderate, severe or life-threatening (if mixed features, treat as the higher level).
Controlled oxygen to keep SpO2 92% or more; use oxygen-driven nebulisers in severe attacks.
No routine chest X-ray, ABG, antibiotics or sedatives.

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate attack (PEF above 50%)
actions: Salbutamol MDI with spacer 6–12 puffs every 20 min for 1 h, then every 2–4 h; OR nebulised 2.5–5 mg every 20 min for 1 h, then every 2 h.
Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg orally (maximum 50 mg) as soon as possible, for 5–7 days.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe attack (PEF 30–50%, RR 25 or more, HR 120 or more, cannot finish sentences)
actions: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5–5 mg back-to-back every 20 min for 1 h, then hourly.
Add ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 20 min for 3 doses, then every 4–6 h (or MDI 4–8 puffs).
IV methylprednisolone 40 mg twice daily (or oral prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg daily, if able to swallow).
Inadequate response: IV magnesium sulphate 1–2 g over 20 min, single dose.
Monitor SpO2; check blood gas if PEF below 30%, electrolytes, glucose and ECG.

clinicalManagement.title: Life-threatening attack
actions: Call ICU; prepare for intubation.
Oxygen to SpO2 92% or more; continuous nebulised salbutamol 10–15 mg with ipratropium 1.5 mg over 1 h (oxygen-driven).
Methylprednisolone 60–80 mg IV every 8–12 h.
Magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 20 min.
ABG, chest X-ray, electrolytes, glucose, ECG.

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess after 1 h and decide disposition
actions: Adequate: PEF above 60%, SpO2 92% or more on air, stable for at least 4 h → discharge track.

Partial: PEF 30–50%, SpO2 92% or more on oxygen → continue salbutamol + ipratropium every 1–4 h; prednisolone 1 mg/kg (maximum 50 mg) or IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day or methylprednisolone 80 mg/day; admit if no adequate response after 4 h.
Poor: PEF below 30%, SpO2 below 92% on high-flow oxygen, fatigue, rising PaCO2 or respiratory acidosis → ICU.
Needs ventilatory support, falling PEF/FEV1, persisting hypoxia, hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis, exhaustion, shallow breathing or drowsiness.

Severe beta-lactam allergy: ciprofloxacin per MOH

pathophysiology.summary: Bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Non-variceal causes (mainly peptic ulcer disease from H. pylori, NSAIDs or aspirin) are most common; variceal bleeding results from portal hypertension in cirrhosis and carries higher mortality.
keyMechanisms: Peptic ulcer: acid–pepsin erosion through a vessel; 'high-risk stigmata' (active bleeding, visible vessel, adherent clot) predict rebleeding.
Varices: portal hypertension diverts blood through fragile oesophageal or gastric collaterals; bleeding is often torrential, and patients are prone to infection, encephalopathy and kidney injury.
Haemoglobin falls late (haemodilution takes hours); urea rises because blood is digested and absorbed.
Antithrombotics (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, warfarin, DOACs) and coagulopathy of liver disease worsen bleeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate
actions: IV access, IV fluids for all; unstable: 500 mL crystalloid bolus in under 15 min (BSG).
Restrictive transfusion: trigger Hb below 70 g/L, target 70–100 g/L (higher trigger in ischaemic heart disease or instability).
Ongoing instability: activate major haemorrhage protocol (blood, platelets, clotting factors) and critical care review.
Platelets if actively bleeding and below 50 × 10⁹/L; do not give platelets if stable and not bleeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Risk-stratify
actions: Calculate GBS. GBS 0–1: consider outpatient management with early endoscopy follow-up.

clinicalManagement.title: Antithrombotics and reversal
actions: Continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention (stop other NSAIDs).
Interrupt P2Y12 inhibitors until haemostasis — if coronary stents, decide with cardiology.
Interrupt warfarin; if actively bleeding give PCC (MOH: dose by INR — e.g. INR 2–2.5: 0.9–1.3 mL/kg Octaplex; maximum single dose 3000 IU) plus vitamin K 5–10 mg IV.

Interrupt DOAC; life-threatening bleeding: idarucizumab (dabigatran) or andexanet alfa (apixaban/rivaroxaban) where available; seek haematology advice. MOH protocol lists PCC for life-threatening DOAC bleeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected variceal bleeding (cirrhosis)
actions: Terlipressin 2 mg IV four times a day (BSG); stop after definitive haemostasis or 5 days (NICE). Caution in ischaemic heart or peripheral vascular disease.
IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 h (MOH prophylaxis in cirrhosis with GI bleeding); oral step-down amoxicillin–clavulanate 500 mg q12h when stable.
Endoscopy: band ligation for oesophageal varices; cyanoacrylate for gastric varices; TIPS if not controlled.

clinicalManagement.title: Endoscopy and non-variceal treatment
actions: No PPI before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal bleeding (NICE).
Endoscopic therapy: mechanical (clips) ± adrenaline, thermal + adrenaline, or fibrin/thrombin + adrenaline — never adrenaline alone.
High-risk stigmata after endoscopy: high-dose IV PPI (e.g. 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 h, or intermittent IV / high-dose oral PPI as alternatives).
Rebleeding: repeat endoscopy; unstable rebleed → interventional radiology, or surgery if IR is not promptly available.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 24 h (immediately after resuscitation if unstable)

pathophysiology.summary: Essential hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identified secondary cause. It is often asymptomatic and increases cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and kidney risk.
keyMechanisms: Interactions among genetic, renal, vascular, neurohormonal, and environmental factors
Increased systemic vascular resistance and altered sodium-volume regulation
Cumulative pressure-related vascular and target-organ injury

pathophysiology.summary: Periodic health examination is a risk-based preventive-care process rather than a disease episode. It identifies modifiable cardiovascular, metabolic, cancer, infectious, mental-health and functional risks before symptoms or irreversible complications develop, while avoiding screening that has an unfavourable balance of benefit and harm.
keyMechanisms: Age, sex, family history, exposures and comorbidity alter baseline disease probability and screening benefit.
Repeated measurement can detect trajectories in blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia and lipids before complications emerge.
Evidence-based screening shifts selected cancers and chronic diseases toward earlier diagnosis.
Shared decisions reduce harms from false positives, overdiagnosis and preventive medicines with small net benefit.

redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, shock, ongoing myocardial ischaemia or severe pulmonary oedema
New focal neurological deficit suggesting stroke
Syncope with a very rapid or very slow ventricular response
Acute decompensated heart failure or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
symptoms: Palpitations or an irregular heartbeat
Breathlessness or reduced exercise tolerance
Fatigue, dizziness, presyncope or syncope
Chest discomfort or presentation with stroke or transient ischaemic attack
physicalSigns: Irregularly irregular pulse
Variable first heart sound and pulse deficit
Tachycardia or, with conduction disease or medication, bradycardia
Signs of heart failure, valve disease or systemic embolism

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Organised flutter activity on electrocardiogram, often with a regular or patterned ventricular response.
Discrete premature P waves with intervening sinus rhythm rather than sustained fibrillatory activity.
At least three P-wave morphologies and an isoelectric baseline, often in severe pulmonary disease.
Consistent P waves and a physiological trigger; careful lead review separates artefact from atrial activity.

ruleIn.testName: 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleIn.modalityTarget: 12-lead electrocardiogram — Atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Irregularly irregular R-R intervals with no consistent discrete P waves.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides rhythm confirmation and identifies conduction, ischaemic or pre-excitation features that alter management.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring — Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Intermittent electrocardiographically documented atrial fibrillation during symptoms or silent episodes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Monitoring duration should match symptom frequency when the resting electrocardiogram is normal.

ruleIn.testName: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Transthoracic echocardiography when indicated — Structural or functional heart disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Atrial enlargement, ventricular dysfunction, valve disease or another finding that changes management.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports rhythm-control planning, heart-failure assessment and selected refinement of thromboembolic risk.

ruleOut.testName: Thyroid function testing
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Thyroid function testing — Thyrotoxicosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No biochemical hyperthyroidism, or a reversible driver is identified.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Thyroid disease can precipitate atrial fibrillation and requires concurrent treatment.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, renal and liver function
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, renal and liver function — Metabolic precipitant or medicine contraindication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No correctable electrolyte disturbance; organ function is adequate for the selected medicine or prompts adjustment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Identifies reversible contributors and is essential before anticoagulant or antiarrhythmic selection.

ruleOut.testName: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Acute coronary and pulmonary assessment when clinically indicated — Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No acute ischaemic or thromboembolic trigger, or one is identified and treated through its urgent pathway.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: New atrial fibrillation may be secondary to another time-critical condition.

pathophysiology.summary: Atrial fibrillation is a supraventricular tachyarrhythmia with disorganised atrial activation and ineffective atrial contraction. Irregular ventricular conduction can cause symptoms or tachycardia-mediated dysfunction, while atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation and systemic embolism.
keyMechanisms: Ectopic atrial triggers and a susceptible atrial substrate sustain chaotic electrical activation.
Loss of coordinated atrial contraction and irregular atrioventricular conduction reduce haemodynamic efficiency.
Blood stasis, endothelial dysfunction and prothrombotic factors increase left-atrial thrombus and stroke risk.
Hypertension, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, sleep apnoea and alcohol can promote onset or recurrence.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stability and reversible triggers
actions: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, ischaemia, heart failure and neurological status.
Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram and correct hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance or another precipitant.
Seek senior cardiology/critical-care support for unstable or pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Perform urgent synchronised electrical cardioversion under the locally approved resuscitation and sedation protocol.
Do not delay emergency cardioversion solely to complete routine anticoagulation assessment.
branches.condition: Life-threatening haemodynamic instability attributable to atrial fibrillation

actions: Proceed to symptom, duration, rate/rhythm and thromboembolic-risk assessment.
branches.condition: No life-threatening instability

clinicalManagement.title: Assess stroke and bleeding risks
actions: Use CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk and a validated bleeding-risk tool such as ORBIT.
Identify and modify reversible bleeding risks rather than using a bleeding score alone to withhold anticoagulation.
Discuss absolute benefits, bleeding harms and patient preferences using shared decision making.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis and whenever risk factors change

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent thromboembolism
actions: Offer an SFDA-authorised generic direct-acting oral anticoagulant, such as dabigatran etexilate or rivaroxaban, when indicated and suitable; select using renal function, interactions, adherence and the local formulary.
Use warfarin when a direct-acting anticoagulant is contraindicated, unsuitable, or the clinical condition specifically requires a vitamin-K antagonist.
Do not use antiplatelet monotherapy solely for atrial-fibrillation stroke prevention.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for all dosing; this record is not a prescribing source.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose rate or rhythm control
actions: Use rate control first for many stable patients, with a generic beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker selected for comorbidity and contraindications.
Consider rhythm control for persistent symptoms, a reversible cause, new onset, atrial flutter suitable for ablation or heart failure thought to be driven by the arrhythmia.
Avoid a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker in acute decompensated heart failure and obtain specialist advice.
Assess anticoagulation requirements around cardioversion according to rhythm duration and the current protocol.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: During initial management and at symptom review

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate persistent or complex disease
actions: Refer for cardiology review when symptoms remain uncontrolled, recurrence follows cardioversion or antiarrhythmic/ablation decisions are needed.
Consider catheter ablation through specialist shared decision making for eligible symptomatic patients.
Reassess stroke prevention after rhythm restoration because apparent sinus rhythm does not automatically remove thromboembolic risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Promptly when initial treatment fails or complexity is identified

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review symptoms, pulse/rate, blood pressure, anticoagulant adherence, bleeding risk and renal function at a medicine-appropriate interval; reassess stroke risk at least annually and whenever age or comorbidity changes.
mdtReferrals: Cardiology or electrophysiology for rhythm-control and ablation decisions
Anticoagulation or clinical pharmacy service for medicine selection, interactions and adherence
Stroke service for any acute or previous cerebrovascular event
Sleep medicine and weight-management services where relevant
lifestyleAndDiet: Support weight management, regular physical activity and control of blood pressure and diabetes.
Screen for and treat obstructive sleep apnoea when suspected.
Reduce excessive alcohol and stimulant exposure and stop smoking.
For warfarin, advise consistency rather than avoidance of vitamin-K-containing foods and arrange INR education.
patientEducation: Explain the irregular rhythm, symptom-control options and the distinct purpose of anticoagulation.
Teach stroke warning signs and the need for immediate emergency assessment.
Provide medicine-specific bleeding, missed-dose, procedure and interaction advice using approved Saudi information.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamics are stable and acute triggers have been addressed.
A rate/rhythm strategy and anticoagulation decision are documented with renal-function-appropriate prescribing.
The patient understands stroke and bleeding precautions and has timely follow-up.

content.specialty: Medical Oncology, Breast Surgery and Radiation Oncology

redFlags: Rapidly progressive inflammatory breast change
Spinal pain with weakness, sensory change or bladder/bowel dysfunction
New focal neurological deficit, seizure or raised intracranial-pressure symptoms
Visceral crisis with organ dysfunction requiring rapid oncology assessment
symptoms: New breast or axillary lump
Nipple retraction or bloody discharge
Persistent focal breast change or skin dimpling
Bone pain, breathlessness, neurological symptoms or weight loss in advanced disease
physicalSigns: Discrete breast mass or asymmetric thickening
Peau d'orange, ulceration or inflammatory change
Nipple inversion or eczematous nipple lesion
Palpable axillary or supraclavicular nodes

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often mobile, well-circumscribed and benign on age-appropriate imaging, but tissue diagnosis is required when assessment is discordant.
Fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound with resolution after aspiration in selected cases.
Pain, erythema, fever and a collection; non-resolution requires investigation for inflammatory malignancy.
History of trauma or surgery with characteristic imaging, although biopsy may be needed if suspicious.

ruleIn.testName: Triple assessment
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Triple assessment — Breast malignancy
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Concordant suspicious clinical examination, mammography/ultrasound and core-biopsy histology.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Integrates anatomy and tissue diagnosis while minimising false reassurance from any single test.

ruleIn.testName: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Histopathology with ER, PR and HER2 testing — Invasive breast-cancer subtype
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Malignant morphology with grade and validated receptor status.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms diagnosis and directs endocrine, anti-HER2 and chemotherapy decisions.

ruleIn.testName: Stage-directed imaging
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Stage-directed imaging — Regional or distant metastatic disease
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Imaging defines tumour, nodal and metastatic burden when stage or symptoms justify it.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Avoids indiscriminate staging in low-risk disease while identifying treatment-changing metastases.

ruleOut.testName: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Image-guided core biopsy of a suspicious benign-appearing lesion — Benign breast disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Pathology is benign and concordant with clinical and imaging findings.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Discordance requires repeat sampling or excision rather than simple reassurance.

ruleOut.testName: Targeted imaging of new symptoms
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Targeted imaging of new symptoms — Metastatic complication
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No metastasis explaining the symptom, or a lesion is identified for urgent management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine surveillance imaging in asymptomatic early-stage survivors is not a substitute for symptom-led assessment.

pathophysiology.summary: Breast cancer comprises malignant epithelial tumours with heterogeneous hormone-receptor, HER2 and genomic biology. Disease may remain in situ, invade breast and regional lymphatics, or spread haematogenously to bone, liver, lung and brain; biology and stage jointly determine treatment and prognosis.
keyMechanisms: Accumulated genomic and epigenetic alterations enable uncontrolled proliferation and invasion.
Oestrogen/progesterone-receptor signalling and HER2 amplification define actionable biological subsets.
Lymphatic spread commonly involves axillary and regional nodes.
Tumour heterogeneity and treatment selection pressure can change receptor status in recurrent disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm pathology and stage
actions: Obtain adequate core tissue and report histological type, grade and ER, PR and HER2 status.
Complete stage-appropriate imaging and assess performance status, comorbidities and baseline organ function.
Arrange genetic and fertility counselling when clinical criteria are met.

clinicalManagement.title: Agree a multidisciplinary plan
actions: Discuss every new case in a breast multidisciplinary conference.
Integrate stage, biology, patient goals, surgical feasibility and treatment toxicities.
Record sequence of surgery, systemic therapy and radiotherapy with responsible teams.

clinicalManagement.title: Deliver local-regional therapy
actions: Offer breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy according to disease extent, contraindications and informed preference.
Stage the axilla using the appropriate sentinel-node or nodal procedure.
Plan radiotherapy according to surgical approach, margins, nodal involvement and recurrence risk.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: According to stage and treatment sequence

clinicalManagement.title: Select biology-directed systemic therapy
actions: Use endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive disease when indicated.
Use generic anti-HER2 therapy for eligible HER2-positive disease with cardiac monitoring.
Select chemotherapy and any contemporary targeted or immunotherapy only through the current approved oncology protocol.
Prioritise neoadjuvant systemic therapy and serial response assessment.
Proceed to local therapy if disease becomes operable and the MDT confirms benefit.
branches.condition: Locally advanced or inflammatory disease

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Neoadjuvant or adjuvant as agreed by MDT

clinicalManagement.title: Survivorship or advanced-disease review
actions: Use interval history, examination and mammography of retained breast tissue according to policy.
Manage endocrine, bone, cardiac, menopausal and lymphoedema effects.
For metastatic disease, prioritise symptom control, quality of life and biology-directed therapy with early supportive care.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After initial treatment and throughout follow-up

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow the current Saudi oncology surveillance schedule, including clinical review and mammography where breast tissue remains; monitor therapy-specific cardiac, bone, gynaecological and lymphoedema risks and investigate new symptoms promptly.
mdtReferrals: Breast surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist and breast-care nurse
Genetics for hereditary-risk criteria
Fertility service before gonadotoxic treatment when relevant
Physiotherapy/lymphoedema, psycho-oncology and palliative care according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Support regular physical activity and maintenance of a healthy body composition during and after treatment.
Provide dietetic advice for treatment-related weight change, nausea or malnutrition.
Offer smoking-cessation support and advise avoidance of unreviewed supplements that may interact with therapy.
patientEducation: Explain stage, receptor status, treatment intent and the role of each modality in plain language.
Discuss expected adverse effects, fertility, sexual health, pregnancy considerations and when to seek urgent care.
Provide individualised information on recurrence symptoms without encouraging harmful routine self-testing.
dischargeCriteria: The diagnosis, stage, receptor profile and MDT plan are documented.

Surveillance ownership, medicine monitoring and urgent symptom pathways are explicit.

content.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia

pitfalls: Waiting for procalcitonin before treating confirmed CAP.
Broad MRSA/Pseudomonas cover for everyone.
Fluoroquinolone without considering TB.
Steroids in non-severe CAP.
Routine follow-up chest X-ray in recovered patients.
keyPoints: Confirm with imaging; grade with PSI and ATS severe criteria.
Inpatient: ceftriaxone + macrolide; severe: ceftriaxone + macrolide or respiratory quinolone.
Add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only with prior isolation or validated risk.
Influenza-positive inpatients: oseltamivir plus antibacterials.
Stop once stable: short courses are enough.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage community-acquired pneumonia in the emergency department.

content.specialty: Internal Medicine, Respiratory Medicine and Infectious Diseases

redFlags: ATS major criteria: septic shock needing vasopressors, or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation — direct ICU admission

Three or more ATS minor criteria: RR 30 or more, PaO2/FiO2 250 or less, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, urea (BUN) 20 mg/dL or more (about 7 mmol/L), WBC below 4 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 100 × 10⁹/L, temperature below 36 °C, hypotension needing aggressive fluids
PSI class V (above 130 points): ICU
symptoms: Cough, sputum, fever, rigors, breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain.
Confusion (a severity criterion).
physicalSigns: Fever (or hypothermia below 36 °C in severe disease), tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia.
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing, dullness to percussion.
Confusion; hypotension.

differentials.condition: Acute bronchitis or viral upper respiratory infection
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No new infiltrate on imaging.
Pleuritic pain and hypoxia without consolidation; VTE risk factors.
Bilateral infiltrates, raised JVP, cardiomegaly, raised natriuretic peptide.
Subacute course, weight loss, upper-lobe or cavitary change; MOH protocol cautions against fluoroquinolones without excluding TB.
Onset 48 h or more after admission; follow the HAP/VAP section and local antibiogram.

evidenceAudit.scope: Immunocompetent adults with CAP. Antibiotic regimens follow the Saudi MOH LRTI protocol (adopted from ATS/IDSA 2019); steroid and duration updates from ATS 2025.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.

pathophysiology.summary: CAP is acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital. Alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate, causing consolidation, impaired gas exchange and, in severe cases, sepsis and respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Organisms reach the alveoli (usually by micro-aspiration) and overwhelm local defences; the inflammatory exudate fills air spaces (consolidation).
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch from consolidated lung causes hypoxaemia and tachypnoea.
The systemic inflammatory response can progress to sepsis, septic shock and multi-organ failure.
Resistant organisms (MRSA, Pseudomonas) are more likely after recent hospitalisation and IV antibiotics or with prior respiratory isolation.
Viral infection (e.g. influenza) can coexist with bacterial infection.

pathophysiology.summary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is clot formation in the deep veins, usually of the leg, which can break off and obstruct the pulmonary arteries. A large obstruction raises right ventricular afterload; the right ventricle dilates and fails, causing obstructive shock.
keyMechanisms: Virchow's triad of stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability drives clot formation; provoking factors include surgery, immobilisation, cancer, pregnancy and hormones.
Proximal (popliteal and above) DVT carries the main embolic risk; distal DVT can extend proximally.
PE obstructs pulmonary flow, causing V/Q mismatch and hypoxaemia, raised pulmonary pressure and right ventricular strain (raised troponin and natriuretic peptides, RV dilatation on echo or CT).
Haemodynamic collapse (high-risk PE) comes from right ventricular failure and falling left ventricular filling.
Recurrence risk depends on whether the event was provoked by a major transient factor, unprovoked, or due to persistent factors (cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess probability and start anticoagulation early
actions: Stabilise first. Use a validated pre-test probability score with D-dimer in stable patients.

Start anticoagulation before confirmation if suspicion is high, or intermediate with results delayed over 4 h, or low with results delayed over 24 h (MOH), unless bleeding or an absolute contraindication.
Bedside echo now; if RV dysfunction and no alternative cause, treat as high-risk PE.

clinicalManagement.title: Respiratory and haemodynamic support
actions: Oxygen to SpO2 at least 90% (MOH); intubate for severe hypoxaemia, collapse or respiratory failure.
Hypotension: small fluid volumes (500–1000 mL 0.9% saline), then noradrenaline if perfusion does not improve; dobutamine sometimes for low output.

clinicalManagement.title: High-risk (massive) PE: reperfusion
actions: Systemic thrombolysis is first-line: alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 h (product information). Use UFH infusion with thrombolysis.
Contraindication to thrombolysis: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment where available; ECMO only as a bridge.
Intermediate-risk PE: no routine thrombolysis; monitor and give rescue thrombolysis if decompensating.

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify stable PE
actions: Intermediate risk: RV strain on imaging and/or raised troponin or BNP → admit, monitor, anticoagulate.
Low risk: sPESI 0 or no Hestia criteria, and no RV dysfunction or right heart thrombus → consider early discharge on a DOAC.
sPESI items (1 point each): age above 80, cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR 110 or more, SBP below 100, SpO2 below 90%.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose the anticoagulant
actions: Stable patients: a DOAC is preferred over warfarin (ESC). Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily.

Parenteral options: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 h (or 1.5 mg/kg every 24 h); IV UFH 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h to target aPTT (preferred if unstable, severe renal failure or thrombolysis planned); fondaparinux by weight (5, 7.5 or 10 mg daily).
Warfarin: overlap with a parenteral agent for at least 5 days and until INR is 2 or more for 2 days; target INR 2–3.
Dabigatran: only after at least 5 days of a parenteral agent.
LMWH, or edoxaban or rivaroxaban (caution in GI cancer).

pitfalls: Starting insulin before the potassium result.
Stopping or cutting insulin because glucose is normal while ketones are still high.
Missing euglycaemic DKA in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Calling infection on a WBC of 12 (stress leucocytosis is expected).
Using urine ketones or the anion gap to call resolution.
Stopping IV insulin without overlapping SC insulin → rebound DKA.
Routine bicarbonate.

keyPoints: D + K + A: all three needed.
Fluids → check potassium → insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h. Never reverse the order.
Treat the ketones, not the glucose: add dextrose, keep insulin running.
Always look for the trigger, most often infection or missed insulin.

Discharge only with sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin supply and follow-up in 2–4 weeks. SDCPG: people with type 2 diabetes who had unexplained ketoacidosis in the 3 months before Ramadan should not fast.

learningObjectives: Diagnose, grade and treat adult DKA in the emergency department.

redFlags: SDCPG markers for HDU/ICU: GCS below 12; pH below 7.1; ketones above 6 mmol/L; bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L; potassium below 3.3 or above 6.0 mmol/L; systolic BP below 90 mmHg; SpO2 below 92% on air; pulse above 100 or below 60; urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h or AKI
Potassium below 3.3 mmol/L (SDCPG) or below 3.5 mmol/L (consensus): hold insulin and replace potassium first
New headache, confusion or falling consciousness during treatment: suspect cerebral oedema; senior help and early brain imaging
Pregnancy, heart failure, dialysis or frail older adult: standard fluid volumes are unsafe
symptoms: Onset: hours to a few days (HHS: days to weeks).
Volume depletion: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness.

Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain in more than half. Abdominal pain correlates with the severity of acidosis and can mimic a surgical abdomen; if it does not settle as the acidosis corrects, look for a surgical cause.
Neurological: most patients are alert; drowsiness, stupor or coma occur in severe DKA and are more common in HHS.
precipitants: Infection: the most common trigger (urinary tract infection and pneumonia most often).
Insulin omission or insufficient insulin: the main cause of recurrent DKA.
SGLT2 inhibitors: can cause euglycaemic DKA.
Acute illness: myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis, surgery; also alcohol and drugs that affect carbohydrate metabolism.
physicalSigns: Dehydration: dry mucosa, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, shock in severe cases.
Respiratory: Kussmaul respiration (deep, rapid breathing) and a fruity acetone breath.
Signs of the trigger: chest, urine, skin or foot infection; features of myocardial infarction or an acute abdomen.
Record GCS: below 12 is an SDCPG severity marker.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Glucose at least 33.3 mmol/L, effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg, ketones below 3.0 mmol/L, pH at least 7.3 and bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L. Older patient, slower onset, confusion common.
Hyperosmolar and ketotic (ketones at least 3.0 mmol/L or pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L). Treat as DKA but lower osmolality slowly.
Intake below about 500 kcal/day; glucose usually not high and acidosis mild.
Heavy alcohol use with a recent binge, vomiting and starvation; glucose may be normal or low.
Pregnant, vomiting; mixed acid–base picture. Involve obstetrics immediately.

differentials.condition: Surgical abdomen, sepsis or MI as the cause
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pain that persists after acidosis corrects, focal abdominal signs, raised lipase with imaging evidence of pancreatitis, ischaemic ECG or raised troponin.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults (SDCPG adult pathway: above 14 years and over 50 kg). Not for children, pregnancy (immediate obstetric input) or haemodynamically unstable patients (ICU). Every number on this page was checked against SDCPG 2021 pp. 71–74, the 2024 international consensus or the 2009 ADA consensus. Clinical approval is pending.
findings: Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
SDCPG and the 2024 consensus differ on several thresholds; both are shown in the comparison table and a local protocol must choose one.

SFDA register (11 Oct 2026): soluble human insulin, insulin glargine, potassium chloride, sodium bicarbonate 8.4%, 0.9% sodium chloride, dextrose and glucagon are registered; no potassium phosphate injection was found.
unverifiedSections: LMWH prophylaxis dose (use the local VTE protocol)
Local choice between SDCPG and consensus thresholds

ruleIn.testName: Capillary / plasma glucose

references.title: Consensus report

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 1–2 h (SDCPG: hourly)
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At least 11.1 mmol/L. Can be below 11.1 in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2 inhibitor, fasting, pregnancy).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnostic criterion. During treatment: add dextrose when it falls to 13–14 mmol/L; below 4.0 mmol/L treat hypoglycaemia.

ruleIn.testName: Blood β-hydroxybutyrate (capillary or serum)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h until resolution
ruleIn.expectedFinding: At least 3.0 mmol/L is diagnostic; above 6.0 mmol/L is severe.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Best marker of diagnosis and resolution (below 0.6 mmol/L). Urine ketones measure acetoacetate, lag behind and can mislead; captopril and valproate cause false positives.

cons: Does not measure oxygenation; use pulse oximetry, or an arterial gas in shock, severe respiratory distress or a suspected mixed acid–base disorder
pros: Faster and less painful than arterial sampling, with lower complication risk
Venous pH and bicarbonate are what the consensus uses for diagnosis, monitoring and resolution
ruleIn.testName: Venous blood gas (pH, bicarbonate)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h until resolution
ruleIn.expectedFinding: pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L (SDCPG: below 15).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Grades severity, sets level of care and tracks resolution (pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L). Bicarbonate therapy only if pH below 7.0 (SDCPG: 6.9).

ruleIn.testName: Potassium

references.title: SDCPG

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Before insulin, 2 h after starting insulin, then every 4 h
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Often normal or high at presentation despite a total-body deficit; falls by 1–2 mmol/L with treatment.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Above 5.2 (SDCPG) / 5.0 (consensus): no added potassium. 3.3–5.2: add 40 mmol/L (SDCPG) or 20–30 mmol/L (consensus). Below 3.3 (SDCPG) / 3.5 (consensus): hold insulin and replace. Target 4–5 mmol/L.

ruleIn.testName: Sodium (corrected for glucose)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Often low because glucose draws water out of cells (translocational, not true hyponatraemia).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Correct for glucose: add about 1.6 mmol/L of sodium for every 5.6 mmol/L of glucose above normal (SDCPG: add 3 per 10 mmol/L above 5.5). A rising sodium as glucose falls is expected and is not a reason for hypotonic fluid.

ruleIn.testName: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Arrival
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 12 mmol/L.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports ketoacidosis; useful where ketone testing is unavailable. Do not use it to judge resolution: large volumes of 0.9% saline cause a hyperchloraemic normal-gap acidosis.

ruleOut.testName: Urea and creatinine

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival, then every 4 h; daily after resolution
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised in up to half (pre-renal AKI).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Usually recovers with fluids. Oliguria or AKI is an SDCPG severity marker and makes potassium replacement riskier.

ruleOut.testName: Serum osmolality (2 × Na + glucose)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival; every 4 h if hyperosmolar
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Above 300 mOsm/kg suggests a hyperosmolar component.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: If raised, lower osmolality by no more than 3–8 mOsm/kg/h and sodium by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h.

ruleOut.testName: Full blood count

references.title: Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes (ADA consensus)

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival
ruleOut.expectedFinding: WBC 10–15 × 10⁹/L is usual in DKA from stress hormones.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Do not assume infection from a modest rise. WBC above 25 × 10⁹/L suggests infection and needs a search.

ruleOut.testName: Phosphate, magnesium, calcium

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival; phosphate every 4 h
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Phosphate often normal at first, then falls with insulin.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Replace phosphate only if below 1.0 mmol/L with muscle weakness or respiratory or cardiac compromise.

ruleOut.testName: ECG ± troponin

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Peaked T waves with high potassium; ischaemic changes if MI is the trigger.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Attach a cardiac monitor and repeat the ECG if potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L (SDCPG order sheet); potassium above 6.0 mmol/L is an SDCPG severity marker.

ruleOut.testName: Infection screen; lipase; pregnancy test; HbA1c

references.title: Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes (ADA consensus)

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Arrival, guided by history
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Positive cultures or urinalysis; raised lipase; positive pregnancy test; high HbA1c.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Blood and urine cultures if infection is suspected. Lipase can rise in DKA without pancreatitis, so interpret with imaging. A high HbA1c means the insulin regimen should be changed before discharge.

ruleOut.testName: Chest X-ray

references.title: SDCPG

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Respiratory symptoms, hypoxia, or no obvious trigger
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Consolidation.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Pneumonia is a leading trigger; listed on the SDCPG adult order sheet.

ruleOut.testName: CT head (non-contrast)

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Altered consciousness out of proportion to the acidosis, focal signs, or deterioration during treatment
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Cerebral oedema (rare in adults, about 30% mortality) or a stroke as the trigger.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: The consensus advises a low threshold for brain imaging when mental status changes.

ruleOut.testName: Abdominal ultrasound or CT

references.title: Consensus report

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Abdominal pain that persists after the acidosis has started to correct
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Appendicitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis or another surgical cause.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: DKA pain should settle with treatment; persistent pain needs further evaluation.

adjustments: Reduce to 0.05 unit/kg/h: consensus at glucose below 13.9; SDCPG at glucose below 6

adjustments: None if K above 5.2
K below 3.3: hold insulin; 40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h (SDCPG) or 10 mmol/h (consensus)

Glucose below 4.0: 25 mL 50% dextrose
