pathophysiology.summary: DKA is a state of cellular starvation and runaway catabolism caused by two failures at once: absolute or relative insulin deficiency and an excess of counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone).

references.title: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report

keyMechanisms: Hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis: without insulin, tissues cannot take up glucose while glucagon drives hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Glucose spills into the urine and pulls water, sodium and potassium with it, causing profound dehydration.
Lipolysis and ketogenesis: fat is broken down to free fatty acids, which the liver oxidises to ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate and acetone).
Acidosis: ketoacids consume bicarbonate, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul breathing is the respiratory compensation.

Potassium paradox: acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium is often normal or high despite a total-body deficit of 3–6 mmol/kg. Insulin drives it back in, so check potassium before insulin.
Euglycaemic DKA: about 10% present with glucose below 11.1 mmol/L, most often with SGLT2 inhibitors, reduced intake, pregnancy or alcohol.
HHS is the other end of the spectrum: enough insulin to prevent ketosis but not hyperglycaemia, so dehydration and hyperosmolality dominate. One-third of crises are mixed DKA–HHS.

actions: ABC, GCS, IV access, weight. Send glucose, ketones, VBG, U&E, FBC before treatment.
Confirm D + K + A. Grade severity. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors.
Severe DKA, any SDCPG marker, HHS or critical trigger → HDU/ICU. Mild–moderate and alert → ED or step-down with close nursing.
ICU; give isotonic saline until BP stabilises. The SDCPG order sheet does not apply.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids first
actions: 0.9% NaCl 1 L over hour 1 (no potassium).
Then 1 L over the next 2 h (no potassium), then 1 L over the next 4 h with potassium, then 100–250 mL/h (SDCPG order sheet; adults over 50 kg, SBP at least 90).
Consensus alternative: 0.9% NaCl or balanced crystalloid 500–1000 mL/h for 2–4 h; correct the deficit over 24–48 h.
250 mL boluses with frequent reassessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Potassium gate, then fixed-rate insulin
actions: Never start insulin before the potassium result.
Fixed-rate IV soluble insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl). No bolus (SDCPG).
Continue the patient's usual long-acting basal insulin.
Recheck potassium 2 h after insulin starts, then every 4 h; keep it at 4–5 mmol/L.
No potassium; recheck in 2 h.

actions: Add 40 mmol KCl per litre, maximum 10 mmol/h (SDCPG). Consensus: 20–30 mmol/L.

actions: Hold insulin, cardiac monitor, ECG.

actions: Start 5–10% dextrose with the saline from the outset so insulin can be given.

clinicalManagement.title: Resolution and switch to subcutaneous insulin
actions: Resolved: ketones below 0.6 mmol/L AND pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L, and eating and drinking. Do not use urine ketones or the anion gap.
Give subcutaneous insulin BEFORE stopping the infusion: SDCPG overlaps the first rapid-acting dose by 1 h; consensus gives basal insulin 1–2 h before stopping.

Likely hyperchloraemic acidosis, not persistent DKA; do not delay the switch for this alone.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Glucose at least 11.1 mmol/L, OR known diabetes at any glucose

guidelineComparison.note: Pick one protocol locally and apply it consistently; do not mix thresholds in one patient. pitfalls: Starting insulin before fluids: circulatory collapse.
Using DKA insulin doses (0.1 unit/kg/h) in pure HHS.
Switching to hypotonic fluid just because sodium rises.
Correcting too fast: cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
Forgetting foot protection and VTE prophylaxis.
keyPoints: Fluids first, insulin late and low (0.05 unit/kg/h).
Correct slowly: osmolality about 5 mOsm/kg/h, sodium no more than 10 mmol/L per 24 h, glucose no more than 5 mmol/L/h.
Rising sodium while osmolality falls is expected.
Thromboprophylaxis and heel protection for everyone.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state in the emergency department.

redFlags: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg: resuscitate first; the SDCPG order sheet does not apply until SBP is at least 90
Falling GCS, seizures or new focal signs, especially during treatment: think cerebral oedema or stroke; consider CT brain
Osmolality falling more than 8 mOsm/kg/h or sodium falling more than 10 mmol/L in 24 h
Potassium below 3.3 mmol/L: hold insulin
Signs of limb ischaemia, DVT, PE or stroke (thrombosis)
symptoms: Develops over days to a week, usually in older adults with type 2 diabetes (can be the first presentation).
Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, weakness, vomiting.
Drowsiness, confusion, seizures or coma; focal neurological signs can occur.
Often co-presents with another acute illness (infection, MI, stroke).
precipitants: Infection (30–60%; pneumonia and urinary tract infection most common).
High-dose steroids and other drugs that raise glucose.
Poor adherence; impaired thirst or limited access to water (frail elderly).
physicalSigns: Severe dehydration: dry mucosa, poor skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension.
Reduced GCS; no Kussmaul breathing (no significant acidosis).
Feet: check for ulcers and pressure areas; these patients are at very high risk of heel ulceration.
Signs of the precipitant: chest, urine, skin infection; stroke; MI.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Ketones at least 3.0 mmol/L with pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18. Onset hours to days, Kussmaul breathing.
Hyperosmolar AND ketotic (ketones at least 3.0, urine ketones 2+ or more, pH below 7.30 or bicarbonate below 18): start insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/h (consensus) and correct osmolality slowly.
Focal signs, fever or neck stiffness out of proportion to the metabolic picture; confusion that does not improve as osmolality falls.
Glucose not markedly raised; osmolality driven by sodium.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with HHS or mixed DKA–HHS. Haemodynamically unstable patients are resuscitated first (ICU). Verified against SDCPG 2021 pp. 75–79 and the 2024 consensus.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: HHS is severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. There is enough insulin to stop ketogenesis but not enough to control glucose, so osmotic diuresis runs for days and the fluid deficit is huge.
keyMechanisms: Relative insulin deficiency plus counter-regulatory hormones: hepatic glucose output rises and uptake falls, so glucose climbs above 30 mmol/L.
Osmotic diuresis: water and electrolytes are lost over days; SDCPG notes the fluid deficit is often over 8 L.
Hyperosmolality: water shifts out of brain cells, causing confusion, seizures and coma. Correcting it too fast reverses the shift and risks cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
Little ketosis: residual insulin suppresses lipolysis, so pH and bicarbonate are usually near normal (pH at least 7.3, bicarbonate at least 15).
Prothrombotic state: dehydration and hyperviscosity raise the risk of arterial and venous thrombosis.
Mortality is about ten times that of DKA (MOH: up to 20%); age, degree of dehydration and comorbidity drive prognosis.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and decide level of care
actions: ABC, cardiac monitor, urinary catheter if needed, foot examination.
SBP below 90: give 0.9% NaCl until SBP is at least 90, then follow the HHS protocol.
Most patients need HDU/ICU-level monitoring; start prophylactic LMWH unless contraindicated.
Mixed DKA–HHS: start insulin now (consensus 0.1 unit/kg/h); otherwise follow this pathway.
branches.condition: Ketones at least 3.0 or pH below 7.3

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids are the main treatment
actions: 0.9% NaCl 1 L over the first hour (no potassium).
Then 0.9% NaCl 250 mL/h with potassium as per the algorithm (about 3 L over the next 11–12 h); aim to replace 4 L in the first 12 h.
Targets: positive balance 2–3 L by 6 h and 3–6 L by 12 h; replace the rest over the next 12 h. Rate not to exceed 250 mL/h on the order sheet.
Elderly, cardiac or renal patients: smaller volumes and frequent review.
Reduce the IV fluid rate by 50%.
branches.condition: Osmolality falling more than 5 mOsm/kg/h

actions: Change to 0.45% NaCl at the same rate.
branches.condition: Osmolality not falling despite positive balance, or corrected Na above 150

actions: Change to 5% dextrose in 0.9% NaCl and halve insulin (see below).
branches.condition: Glucose below 13 mmol/L

clinicalManagement.title: Insulin: late and low
actions: Fluid alone lowers glucose a lot in HHS. SDCPG: start insulin only after at least 1 L of fluid and if glucose is not falling, fluid balance is already positive, or there is significant ketosis.
Fixed rate 0.05 unit/kg/h (50 units in 50 mL 0.9% NaCl); never more than 0.05 unit/kg/h (e.g. 4 units/h in 80 kg).
Glucose below 13 mmol/L: reduce to 0.025 unit/kg/h. Glucose 5 mmol/L or less: add 10% dextrose at 50–100 mL/h; do not stop insulin.
Aim for glucose 10–15 mmol/L; fall no faster than 5 mmol/L/h.
Hold insulin for 2 h or until K is at least 3.3; replace potassium (40 mmol in 500 mL over 4 h, max 10 mmol/h).
branches.condition: Potassium below 3.3

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent complications
actions: Thromboprophylaxis with LMWH for all unless contraindicated; SDCPG suggests considering full anticoagulation.
Heel protectors and daily foot checks in neuropathy, deformity or vascular disease.
Treat the precipitant; antibiotics when infection is shown.

clinicalManagement.title: Recovery and transition
actions: Correction usually takes longer than 24 h; do not chase normal values quickly.
Consensus resolution: osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h, cognition improved, glucose below 13.9 mmol/L.
Stop IV insulin once eating and drinking; most need subcutaneous insulin; some newly diagnosed or previously well-controlled patients can later go back to oral agents.
All patients see a diabetes educator.

Osm below 300, urine above 0.5 mL/kg/h, cognition improved, glucose below 13.9

content.title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
content.specialty: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine and Cardiology

redFlags: Blood pressure at or above the severe range with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, acute kidney injury or heart failure
Pregnancy or possible pregnancy with severe hypertension or concerning symptoms
Acute focal neurological deficit or aortic-dissection features
Suspected catecholamine crisis or another rapidly progressive secondary cause
symptoms: Usually asymptomatic and detected on screening
Headache or dizziness, which are non-specific
Symptoms of target-organ disease such as exertional chest discomfort, breathlessness or neurological episodes
Features suggesting a secondary cause, including episodic palpitations, muscle weakness or sleep apnoea
physicalSigns: Repeated elevated clinic blood pressure using correct technique
Postural blood-pressure fall in older adults, diabetes or symptomatic patients
Retinal vascular change
Signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or endocrine disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Raised clinic readings with normal validated ambulatory or home averages.
Normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office averages or unexplained target-organ damage.
Young onset, abrupt worsening, resistant disease, hypokalaemia, renal findings, endocrine features or a medicine/substance trigger.
Pain, anxiety, acute illness or recent stimulant exposure with normal readings after the driver resolves.

ruleIn.testName: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Standardised repeated clinic blood pressure — Persistent clinic hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Clinic blood pressure remains at or above the diagnostic threshold after repeat measurement with correct cuff and positioning.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Technique and repetition reduce random error and identify inter-arm difference.

ruleIn.testName: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Ambulatory blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average waking readings meet the validated diagnostic threshold using adequate measurements.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Preferred confirmation method for clinic readings below the severe range and distinguishes white-coat effect.

ruleIn.testName: Home blood-pressure monitoring
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Home blood-pressure monitoring — Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Average readings after discarding the first day meet the validated home threshold.
ruleIn.targetCondition: Sustained hypertension when ABPM is unsuitable
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Provides confirmation and supports later self-monitoring when performed with a validated device and protocol.

ruleOut.testName: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio and urinalysis — Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No albuminuria or haematuria, or an abnormality prompts renal evaluation.
ruleOut.targetCondition: Chronic kidney disease or renal target-organ damage
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Renal disease can be both a cause and consequence of hypertension and changes treatment choice and targets.

ruleOut.testName: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, glycated haemoglobin and lipid profile — Secondary contributor and cardiovascular comorbidity
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Baseline metabolic and renal status is defined; hypokalaemia, kidney dysfunction or diabetes redirects assessment.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Supports cardiovascular-risk estimation and safe medicine selection.

ruleOut.testName: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Fundoscopy and 12-lead electrocardiogram — Retinal or cardiac target-organ damage
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No hypertensive retinopathy or left-ventricular/cardiac abnormality, or damage is documented for risk management.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Target-organ damage changes urgency and the balance of treatment benefit.

pathophysiology.summary: Sustained arterial hypertension reflects increased systemic vascular resistance, altered sodium-volume balance and neurohormonal activation interacting with age, genetics, adiposity and environmental exposures. Chronic pressure load accelerates vascular remodelling and damages the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and peripheral arteries.
keyMechanisms: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic activation increase vascular tone and sodium retention.
Endothelial dysfunction and arterial stiffness raise systolic pressure and pulse pressure.
Renal sodium handling and pressure natriuresis reset at a higher arterial pressure.
Persistent load causes left-ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy and cerebrovascular injury.

clinicalManagement.title: Measure and confirm
actions: Use a validated, maintained device, correct cuff size, supported arm and a quiet seated setting.
Measure both arms initially and use the arm with the persistently higher reading.
Confirm clinic hypertension with ambulatory monitoring or, when unsuitable, structured home monitoring unless urgent severe hypertension requires immediate assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Identify severe hypertension requiring urgent assessment
actions: Assess for retinal, neurological, cardiac, aortic and renal target-organ injury.
Use emergency transfer for life-threatening symptoms or suspected acute organ injury.
Do not rapidly lower asymptomatic blood pressure outside a monitored, indication-specific protocol.
Activate emergency specialist management and monitored intravenous therapy under the local protocol.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure with acute target-organ injury

actions: Arrange urgent clinical review, confirm adherence and complete prompt organ assessment rather than routine follow-up.
branches.condition: Severe blood pressure without acute target-organ injury

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Same day when severe readings or symptoms are present

clinicalManagement.title: Assess cardiovascular risk and organ damage
actions: Obtain urine albumin-creatinine ratio, haematuria screen, glycated haemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR and lipids.
Perform fundoscopy and a 12-lead electrocardiogram.
Use a cardiovascular-risk tool validated or approved for local Saudi practice and assess for secondary-cause clues.

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifestyle and pharmacological treatment
actions: Offer lifestyle intervention to every patient and discuss medicine using age, diabetes, kidney disease, pregnancy potential, frailty and cardiovascular risk.
Use generic ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, calcium-channel blockers or thiazide-like diuretics in the guideline sequence when suitable and SFDA authorised.
Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an angiotensin-receptor blocker.
Use current SFDA labelling and the local formulary for dose, contraindication and monitoring decisions; this record is not a prescribing source.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: After confirmed diagnosis, sooner when severity or organ damage requires

clinicalManagement.title: Titrate and monitor
actions: Check adherence, side effects, postural symptoms and validated clinic or home readings before intensification.
Monitor kidney function and electrolytes after renin-angiotensin system blockers, diuretics or mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists according to protocol.
Before labelling resistant hypertension, confirm out-of-office elevation, optimal tolerated triple therapy and adherence, then seek specialist input or use protocol-directed fourth-line treatment.
Individualise targets for frailty, multimorbidity and significant postural hypotension.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At defined intervals after each treatment change and at least annually once stable

nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review after initiation or each medicine change until a stable target is achieved, then provide at least annual review of blood pressure, postural symptoms, lifestyle, adherence, adverse effects, renal function and evolving cardiovascular risk.
mdtReferrals: Primary-care pharmacist or nurse for adherence and home-monitoring support
Nephrology, endocrinology or hypertension specialist for suspected secondary or resistant hypertension
Obstetric medicine for pregnancy, pregnancy planning or postpartum hypertension
Dietitian, weight-management and smoking-cessation services according to need
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce dietary sodium using culturally relevant food choices; avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes when kidney disease, diabetes or interacting medicines make them unsafe.
Encourage regular aerobic and strengthening activity and gradual weight reduction when indicated.
Limit excessive caffeine and alcohol, stop smoking and address sleep apnoea risk.
Do not recommend calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements solely to lower blood pressure.
patientEducation: Explain that hypertension is often silent but treatment reduces long-term cardiovascular and renal risk.
Teach validated home-monitoring technique and how to record readings without excessive repeated checking.
Discuss medicine purpose, common adverse effects, pregnancy precautions and when to seek urgent care.
dischargeCriteria: Hypertension is confirmed or excluded using an appropriate out-of-office pathway.
Target-organ and cardiovascular-risk assessment is complete or has a named owner.
Treatment, monitoring, individual target and urgent symptom advice are documented and understood.

pitfalls: Labetalol in asthma.
Diazepam or phenytoin instead of magnesium.
Fluid overload (pulmonary oedema).
Steroids to treat HELLP.
Continuing methyldopa after birth (depression).
keyPoints: Aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks for high-risk women.
Treat 140/90 and above; target 135/85; severe 160/110 is an emergency.
Labetalol first, nifedipine if asthma, methyldopa third.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/h for 24 h.
Birth at 37 weeks for pre-eclampsia; enalapril postnatally.

symptoms: Often asymptomatic (detected at routine BP check).

pathophysiology.summary: Pre-eclampsia is a placental disorder: abnormal remodelling of the spiral arteries leads to placental ischaemia, which releases anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1, low placental growth factor) that cause widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction — hypertension, proteinuria and multi-organ injury.
keyMechanisms: Endothelial dysfunction → vasoconstriction, capillary leak (oedema, pulmonary oedema), platelet activation and coagulation (HELLP, DIC).
Low placental growth factor (PlGF) reflects placental dysfunction — PlGF-based testing helps rule out pre-eclampsia (20 to 36+6 weeks).

Organ involvement: kidney (creatinine 90 µmol/L or more, proteinuria), liver (transaminases above 40 IU/L, capsule stretch → epigastric/RUQ pain), brain (headache, visual disturbance, clonus, eclampsia, stroke), blood (platelets below 150 × 10⁹/L, haemolysis), placenta (fetal growth restriction, abnormal Doppler, stillbirth).
Severe hypertension (160/110 or higher) risks intracerebral haemorrhage and is treated urgently.
Delivery of the placenta is the only cure; disease can present or worsen after birth.

clinicalManagement.title: Prevention
actions: Aspirin 75–150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth if 1 high-risk factor (previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension) or more than 1 moderate risk factor (first pregnancy, age 40 or over, interval above 10 years, BMI 35 or more, family history, multiple pregnancy).
Stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs (within 2 working days of pregnancy confirmation) and switch.

clinicalManagement.title: Hypertension — non-severe (140/90 to 159/109)
actions: Treat chronic, gestational and pre-eclampsia hypertension above 140/90; target 135/85 mmHg.
First-line labetalol; nifedipine if labetalol unsuitable (e.g. asthma); methyldopa if neither suitable (NICE).

MOH oral doses: labetalol 100–400 mg two to three times daily (max 1200 mg/day); nifedipine 10–20 mg two to three times daily (max 180 mg/day); methyldopa 250–500 mg two to four times daily (max 2 g/day).
Pre-eclampsia: admit if any concern (severe BP, abnormal bloods, impending eclampsia, fetal compromise); consider fullPIERS/PREP-S.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe hypertension (160/110 or higher)
actions: Admit; treat until below 160/110 then to 135/85.
Labetalol 20 mg IV, then 20–80 mg every 30 min, or infusion 1–2 mg/min, maximum 300 mg, then switch to oral (MOH).
Or oral nifedipine 10 mg every 45 min, maximum 80 mg/day (MOH).
Or hydralazine 5 mg IV, repeat 5–10 mg every 30 min, maximum 20 mg (MOH); give up to 500 mL crystalloid before/with the first dose (NICE).
Limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/h in severe pre-eclampsia (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Magnesium sulfate
actions: Give if eclampsia, or severe pre-eclampsia with birth planned within 24 h, or severe features (headache, scotomata, vomiting, epigastric pain, oliguria with severe hypertension, worsening bloods).
Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen: 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h for 24 h (24 h after the last fit). Recurrent fit: further 2–4 g over 5–15 min (NICE). MOH: 4–6 g over 15–20 min then 1–2 g/h.
Monitor reflexes, RR, SpO2, urine output; toxicity → stop and give calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over 5–10 min.
Do not use diazepam or phenytoin instead of magnesium for eclampsia.
Call for help, left lateral, airway, oxygen; magnesium loading dose; control BP; stabilise then plan birth.
branches.condition: Eclamptic seizure

clinicalManagement.title: Timing of birth (pre-eclampsia)
actions: Before 34 weeks: continue surveillance unless indications for birth; give IV magnesium sulfate and antenatal corticosteroids if early birth planned.
34 to 36+6 weeks: surveillance unless indications; weigh maternal/fetal condition and neonatal cot availability.
37 weeks onwards: initiate birth within 24–48 h.
Do not use steroids to treat HELLP.

clinicalManagement.title: Postnatal care
actions: Measure BP daily for 2 days, once on days 3–5, and when treatment changes; target below 140/90.
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of birth; enalapril first-line postnatally (check creatinine and potassium); nifedipine or amlodipine for women of Black African/Caribbean origin.
Review at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks.

pathophysiology.summary: Maternal sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection during pregnancy, childbirth, the post-abortion period or the postpartum period. A dysregulated host response causes vasodilatation, capillary leak, myocardial depression and microvascular thrombosis; normal pregnancy physiology masks early signs.
keyMechanisms: Pregnancy raises heart rate and lowers BP and WBC thresholds overlap with normal values — most women who died of sepsis were afebrile and had delayed escalation (SMFM).

Common sources: antepartum — pyelonephritis, pneumonia, chorioamnionitis; postpartum — endometritis, wound infection, mastitis, urinary tract infection. Necrotising soft-tissue infection and group A Streptococcus cause rapid toxin-mediated shock.
Lactate rises with tissue hypoperfusion; uterine infection may need delivery/evacuation for source control.
Sepsis increases thrombotic risk (pregnancy is already prothrombotic) — give pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in septic shock.
Fetal compromise usually reflects maternal hypoperfusion — resuscitating the mother is the best fetal treatment.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and escalate
actions: Consider sepsis with any unexplained organ dysfunction and suspected infection — even without fever.
Treat as an emergency: senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, critical care; HDU/ICU for septic shock (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: First hour
actions: Oxygen to maintain saturation; left lateral tilt if pregnant beyond 20 weeks.
Blood and source cultures, lactate — then broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 h.
Hypotension or hypoperfusion: 1–2 L balanced crystalloid within the first 3 h (SMFM); reassess with dynamic measures (avoid overload — pulmonary oedema risk in pregnancy). No starches or gelatin.

clinicalManagement.title: Empiric antibiotics by likely source (SMFM Table 4)
actions: Unknown source or septic shock: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h (or a carbapenem) ± vancomycin if MRSA risk.
Chorioamnionitis: ampicillin + gentamicin; add clindamycin or metronidazole if caesarean birth.
Endometritis: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole (or clindamycin); alternatively ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + metronidazole.
Pyelonephritis: gentamicin + ampicillin, or carbapenem / piperacillin–tazobactam monotherapy.
Community-acquired pneumonia: ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime/ertapenem/ampicillin) + azithromycin.
Necrotising soft-tissue infection: vancomycin + piperacillin–tazobactam; if group A Streptococcus or Clostridium: penicillin G + clindamycin.
Narrow to cultures; shorter courses are usually adequate once source controlled.

clinicalManagement.title: Septic shock
actions: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in pregnancy and postpartum; target MAP 65 mmHg.
Persistent vasopressor need: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (50 mg every 6 h or infusion).
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) in septic shock.
Insulin if glucose above 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L).

clinicalManagement.title: Source control and delivery
actions: Rapidly identify/exclude an anatomical source; drain abscesses, debride necrotising infection.
Uterine source (intra-amniotic infection, retained products): prompt delivery or evacuation regardless of gestation.
Sepsis alone is not an indication for immediate delivery — decide on gestation and maternal/fetal condition; stabilise the mother first. Give antenatal steroids if preterm birth is likely.

pathophysiology.summary: PPH is excessive bleeding after birth — primary within 24 h, secondary from 24 h to 12 weeks. The '4 Ts' are tone (uterine atony, about 80%), trauma (cervix, vagina, uterine rupture), tissue (retained placenta) and thrombin (coagulopathy).
keyMechanisms: After placental separation, bleeding from the placental bed is controlled mainly by myometrial contraction compressing spiral arteries ('living ligatures'); atony removes this control.
Uterine blood flow at term is about 600–700 mL/min (stable physiology), so atony can cause massive loss within minutes.
Pregnancy hypervolaemia masks loss: tachycardia and hypotension appear late; shock index above 1 is an early warning.
Massive bleeding consumes and dilutes clotting factors — fibrinogen falls early; coagulopathy (DIC) worsens bleeding.

Risk factors: placental abruption, placenta praevia/accreta, multiple pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, prolonged labour, operative delivery, retained placenta, over-distended uterus, multiparity — but most PPH has no identifiable risk factor (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevention — third stage of labour
actions: Uterotonic for all births: oxytocin 10 IU IM or IV (WHO first choice), or heat-stable carbetocin 100 µg IM/IV; misoprostol 400–600 µg oral if neither is available.
MOH: oxytocin 5 IU IV or 10 IU IM, with methylergometrine 0.2 mg if no contraindication; controlled cord traction.
Crossmatch blood ready for women with risk factors.
Tranexamic acid is NOT recommended for prevention (WHO).

clinicalManagement.title: First-response bundle (within 15 min of diagnosis)
actions: Call for help: senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, blood bank; one person records times, drugs, fluids and vital signs.
Uterine massage; empty the bladder (Foley catheter).
Oxytocin 10 IU IV slowly over 1–2 min (or in a small volume over 5–10 min), then 10–20 IU infusion over 4 h (WHO). MOH: oxytocin 40 IU in 500 mL Ringer's lactate.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min, within 3 h of birth; repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min or restarts within 24 h.
Two large-bore IV cannulas; isotonic crystalloid (not colloid); oxygen 10–15 L/min; keep warm.
Examine the genital tract for trauma; check the placenta is complete.

clinicalManagement.title: If bleeding continues — second-line uterotonics
actions: Methylergometrine 0.2 mg IM, repeat as needed (not if hypertensive or pre-eclamptic).
Carboprost 0.25 mg IM every 15 min, maximum 8 doses (2 mg) — not in asthma.
Misoprostol 800 µg sublingual (WHO) or 1000 µg rectal (MOH).
Transfuse early: aim Hb above 8 g/dL, platelets above 75, PT below 1.5× normal, fibrinogen above 1 g/L (MOH).
Activate the massive transfusion protocol; arterial/central lines; ICU.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory bleeding
actions: Bimanual uterine compression or external aortic compression as a temporising measure.
Uterine balloon tamponade (e.g. Bakri) after excluding retained tissue and trauma.
Retained placenta: manual removal under anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotics.
Laparotomy: B-Lynch compression suture, uterine then internal iliac artery ligation, embolisation if available; hysterectomy as the last resort (two consultants, family informed — MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: After control
actions: ICU or HDU monitoring; repeat Hb, coagulation, renal function.
Maintenance oxytocin infusion for 4 h.
Thromboprophylaxis once bleeding has stopped (see VTE in pregnancy topic).
Debrief and complete documentation.

pathophysiology.summary: Prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) is rupture of the fetal membranes before the onset of labour; P-PROM is PROM before 37 weeks. Membrane weakening from infection/inflammation, stretch and collagen degradation leads to rupture; the main risks are ascending infection, cord prolapse, abruption and preterm birth.
keyMechanisms: Loss of the amniotic barrier allows ascending infection (chorioamnionitis) — the main maternal consequence (MOH).
Antibiotics after P-PROM prolong the latency period and improve neonatal outcomes.
Corticosteroids (24–34 weeks) reduce respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis.
Prolonged oligohydramnios at very early gestation risks pulmonary hypoplasia and limb contractures.
Term PROM: induction reduces time to birth and chorioamnionitis/endometritis (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and look for reasons to deliver
actions: Speculum for pooling; IGFBP-1/PAMG-1 if none seen.
Deliver regardless of gestation if intra-amniotic infection, significant abruption, cord prolapse, active labour with severe bleeding, life-threatening maternal disease or fetal death (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: P-PROM 24–33+6 weeks: expectant management
actions: Antibiotics: erythromycin 250 mg orally 4 times a day for up to 10 days or until established labour (NICE); oral penicillin if erythromycin not tolerated.

MOH alternative: ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 h + erythromycin 250 mg every 6 h for 48 h, then amoxicillin 250 mg + erythromycin 250 mg every 8 h for 5 days; penicillin allergy: clindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 h + gentamicin 7 mg/kg (ideal body weight) 2 doses 24 h apart, then clindamycin 300 mg orally every 8 h for 5 days.
Corticosteroids: dexamethasone 12 mg IM every 12 h × 2.
Magnesium neuroprotection if birth expected under 30 weeks (32 weeks per MOH).
Monitor for infection, abruption, cord prolapse and fetal wellbeing; consider delivery at 34 weeks (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: P-PROM below 24 weeks
actions: Expectant management if stable; antibiotics and steroids not recommended before viability (MOH); outpatient follow-up possible, admit at viability.

clinicalManagement.title: Term PROM
actions: Induction of labour reduces time to birth and infection (MOH); no routine prophylactic antibiotics at term.
Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis if indicated.

pathophysiology.summary: Preterm labour is regular painful contractions with cervical change before 37 completed weeks. Causes include infection/inflammation (chorioamnionitis), uterine over-distension (multiple pregnancy, polyhydramnios), decidual haemorrhage (abruption), cervical insufficiency and stress pathways; prematurity is a leading cause of neonatal death.
keyMechanisms: Inflammation (cytokines, prostaglandins) ripens the cervix and triggers myometrial contractions — the basis for prostaglandin-synthetase inhibitors and oxytocin antagonists as tocolytics.
Tocolysis does not improve neonatal outcome itself; it buys up to 48 h for corticosteroids and in-utero transfer.
Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate surfactant production and lung maturation, reducing respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis.
Magnesium sulfate before birth under 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy (neuroprotection).
Risk markers: previous preterm birth or mid-trimester loss, short cervix (25 mm or less at 16–24 weeks) — prevention with vaginal progesterone or cerclage (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and diagnose
actions: Senior obstetrician and neonatal team decide the plan; arrange in-utero transfer if needed.
29+6 weeks or less: treat as preterm labour. 30+0 weeks or more: cervical length (or fetal fibronectin) to decide.

clinicalManagement.title: Corticosteroids
actions: Offer at 24+0 to 33+6 weeks; consider at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks; discuss at 22+0 to 23+6 weeks (NICE).
Dexamethasone 12 mg IM every 12 h × 2 (MOH). One repeat course only if the first was more than 7 days ago and still under 34 weeks; never more than 2 courses.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as preterm birth likely

clinicalManagement.title: Tocolysis (to allow steroids/transfer, up to 48 h)
actions: Nifedipine: offer at 26+0 to 33+6 weeks, consider at 24+0 to 25+6 weeks (NICE). MOH dose: 20 mg orally, then 10–20 mg every 6–8 h for up to 48 h.
If nifedipine contraindicated: atosiban 6.75 mg IV over 1 min, then 18 mg/h for 3 h, then 6 mg/h for up to 45 h (maximum 330 mg).
Do not use betamimetics (NICE) — oral terbutaline must not be used for tocolysis (FDA boxed warning). Indomethacin (MOH option at 24–32 weeks) carries fetal ductal and renal risks.
No tocolysis with chorioamnionitis, abruption, fetal compromise or advanced labour.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset with circulatory and cellular/metabolic failure severe enough to raise mortality substantially (above 40% in hospital).
keyMechanisms: Dysregulated host response: the inflammatory and anti-inflammatory response to infection injures the patient's own organs, not just the infected site.
Organ dysfunction: identified as an acute rise in SOFA score of 2 or more (about 10% mortality in a general ward population with suspected infection).
Circulatory failure: vasodilation and capillary leak cause hypotension; tissue hypoperfusion raises lactate and slows capillary refill.
Septic shock: vasopressor needed to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg AND lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid.
Time matters: early antimicrobials are among the most effective ways to reduce mortality; observational data link delays beyond 3–5 h with higher mortality even without shock.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and start immediately
actions: Sepsis and septic shock are emergencies: begin treatment and resuscitation immediately.
Screen acutely ill patients with a tool such as NEWS, MEWS or SIRS; do not rely on qSOFA alone.
Measure lactate; send blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them.

clinicalManagement.title: Antimicrobials
actions: Septic shock or high likelihood of sepsis: give antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition.
Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment for infection vs other causes; if concern persists, antimicrobials within 3 h.
Choose by likely source and local antibiogram (MOH LRTI, UTI and intra-abdominal infection protocols). Add MRSA cover only if high MRSA risk; two Gram-negative agents only if high MDR risk.
Give beta-lactams as a prolonged infusion after an initial bolus; dose by PK/PD principles.
Empiric antifungal therapy (SSC suggests).
branches.condition: High risk of fungal infection

actions: Defer antimicrobials and monitor closely.
branches.condition: Low likelihood of infection and no shock

clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 h if shock or high likelihood of sepsis

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid resuscitation
actions: Sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock: at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 h.
Balanced crystalloid preferred to 0.9% saline; consider albumin after large crystalloid volumes; avoid starches and gelatin.
Reassess after each bolus with dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke volume), capillary refill and lactate.

clinicalManagement.title: Vasopressors to MAP 65
actions: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) first-line; start peripherally (short term, vein at or above the antecubital fossa) rather than waiting for a central line.
Target MAP 65 mmHg initially. Arterial line as soon as practical.
Add vasopressin rather than escalating noradrenaline.

branches.condition: Still inadequate on noradrenaline + vasopressin

clinicalManagement.title: Source control and level of care
actions: Drain abscesses, debride infected tissue, relieve obstruction; remove infected intravascular devices after new access is established.
Patients needing ICU: admit within 6 h.
Hypoxaemic respiratory failure: high-flow nasal oxygen rather than NIV.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing care
actions: Reassess daily for antibiotic de-escalation; use the shortest effective course once the source is controlled.
Start insulin if glucose is 10 mmol/L or more (target 8–10 mmol/L).
Restrictive transfusion (trigger haemoglobin 70 g/L in most patients).
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH preferred); stress ulcer prophylaxis if risk factors for GI bleeding.
Do not give IV vitamin C; no bicarbonate for lactic acidosis unless pH 7.2 or less with AKI stage 2–3.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset with circulatory and cellular/metabolic failure severe enough to raise mortality substantially (above 40% in hospital).
keyMechanisms: Dysregulated host response: the inflammatory and anti-inflammatory response to infection injures the patient's own organs, not just the infected site.
Organ dysfunction: identified as an acute rise in SOFA score of 2 or more (about 10% mortality in a general ward population with suspected infection).
Circulatory failure: vasodilation and capillary leak cause hypotension; tissue hypoperfusion raises lactate and slows capillary refill.
Septic shock: vasopressor needed to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg AND lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid.
Time matters: early antimicrobials are among the most effective ways to reduce mortality; observational data link delays beyond 3–5 h with higher mortality even without shock.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and start immediately

Empiric antifungal therapy (SSC suggests).

pathophysiology.summary: Hypoglycaemia is the commonest acute complication of insulin and sulfonylurea treatment. When glucose falls, adrenergic warning symptoms come first; if glucose keeps falling the brain is starved of glucose (neuroglycopenia), causing confusion, seizures and coma.
keyMechanisms: Too much insulin effect relative to glucose supply: missed meals or fasting, exercise, weight loss, or reduced insulin clearance in kidney failure.
Adrenergic phase (autonomic): palpitations, sweating, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, tingling, hunger.
Neuroglycopenic phase: dizziness, headache, blurred vision, poor concentration, behaviour change or aggression, confusion, seizures, coma.
Hypoglycaemia unawareness: repeated episodes blunt the adrenergic response, so warning symptoms are lost; risk of severe hypoglycaemia rises six-fold.
Long-acting sulfonylureas (e.g. glibenclamide) keep stimulating insulin release, so hypoglycaemia recurs for 24–48 h.

Clinical expression and progression vary with baseline risk, comorbidity, treatment exposure, and access to timely care.

content.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Longitudinal Care Pathway

redFlags: Altered mental status, severe dehydration, or inability to maintain intake
Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or suspected metabolic crisis
Severe hypoglycaemia or infected, ischaemic, or ulcerated foot
symptoms: May be asymptomatic and found on screening
Increased thirst, urination, or hunger
Fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections, or unintentional weight change
physicalSigns: Central adiposity or other metabolic risk features
Acanthosis nigricans in some patients
Possible peripheral sensory loss, foot lesions, or vascular disease

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: May have rapid onset, ketosis, or insulin deficiency; investigate classification when uncertain.
Temporal association with glucocorticoids or other glucose-affecting medicines.
Pancreatic disease, endocrinopathy, or another underlying cause suggested by history or course.
Occurs during acute illness and may resolve; confirm persistent diabetes when appropriate.

pathophysiology.summary: Type 2 diabetes is chronic hyperglycaemia associated with insulin resistance and progressive impairment of insulin secretion, with risk of vascular and other complications.
keyMechanisms: Reduced insulin sensitivity in liver, muscle, and adipose tissue
Progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction
Chronic hyperglycaemia contributing to microvascular and macrovascular injury

topics.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

content.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Pregnancy and Postpartum

pitfalls: Using D-dimer alone to exclude VTE in pregnancy.
Withholding CTPA/V/Q out of radiation concern when PE is suspected.
Multi-dose LMWH vials (preservative) in pregnancy.
Neuraxial anaesthesia within the LMWH window.
Forgetting postnatal prophylaxis after caesarean birth.
keyPoints: Score VTE risk at booking, admission and after birth.
Enoxaparin prophylaxis by weight band; 10 days or 6 weeks postnatally.
Treat with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily; start before imaging.
No warfarin or DOACs in pregnancy.
Stop LMWH 24 h before planned birth; restart 6 h (vaginal) or 12 h (caesarean).

pathophysiology.summary: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad): raised clotting factors and fibrinogen, reduced protein S and fibrinolysis, venous stasis from progesterone and uterine compression of the iliac veins, and vessel injury at delivery. Risk is highest postpartum, especially after caesarean birth.
keyMechanisms: Hypercoagulability is physiological preparation for blood loss at birth and persists for about 6 weeks postpartum.
Left iliac vein compression explains the predominance of left-sided and iliofemoral DVT in pregnancy.
Added risks: previous VTE, thrombophilia, obesity, age over 35, parity 3 or more, caesarean section, PPH, pre-eclampsia, infection, immobility, IVF/OHSS, hyperemesis (MOH/RCOG tool).
D-dimer rises through pregnancy — above 500 µg/L in up to 25% in the third trimester — so it cannot be used alone (ESC).
Warfarin crosses the placenta (teratogenic, fetal bleeding); heparins do not — LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess risk at every stage
actions: Score with the MOH/RCOG obstetric tool; reassess on admission and after delivery.
Low risk: mobilise, avoid dehydration. Intermediate/high risk: LMWH plus mechanical methods.
Avoid or delay pharmacological prophylaxis in women at risk of bleeding after weighing risks.

clinicalManagement.title: Thromboprophylaxis
actions: Enoxaparin once daily by weight: below 50 kg 20 mg; 50–90 kg 40 mg; 91–130 kg 60 mg; 131–170 kg 80 mg; above 170 kg 0.6 mg/kg/day (MOH). UFH 5000 units SC twice daily is the alternative.
Antenatal: high risk from first trimester; intermediate from 28 weeks. Postnatal: at least 10 days; 6 weeks if on antenatal LMWH.
LMWH is safe with breastfeeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected DVT or PE
actions: Start treatment-dose LMWH while awaiting imaging unless contraindicated (stabilise and anticoagulate before confirmation — MOH PE approach).
Use a formal pregnancy diagnostic pathway: clinical probability, D-dimer within the algorithm, leg compression ultrasound, then CTPA or V/Q scan.
Unstable PE: same emergency algorithm as non-pregnant (oxygen to SpO2 90% or more, consider reperfusion).

clinicalManagement.title: Treatment of confirmed VTE
actions: LMWH (prefilled single-dose syringes — multi-dose vials contain preservatives and are contraindicated): enoxaparin 1 mg/kg every 12 h (MOH).
CrCl below 30 mL/min: UFH (IV 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/h, or SC) instead of LMWH.
No warfarin in pregnancy (teratogenic); no rivaroxaban or apixaban in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Fondaparinux if heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Throughout pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum

clinicalManagement.title: Labour and birth
actions: Stop LMWH at least 24 h before planned delivery; no neuraxial anaesthesia if fully anticoagulated when labour starts.
VTE within the last month: switch to IV UFH (stop 4–6 h before delivery). Preterm delivery risk: switch to IV UFH at 36 weeks (MOH).
Restart LMWH 6 h after vaginal birth or 12 h after caesarean if no significant bleeding.
Postpartum: LMWH or warfarin (both safe with breastfeeding).
